Description: Cabot Cape Breton operates dedicated, employer-provided staff housing near its resort properties in Inverness, including purpose-built accommodations and blocks of local rentals secured for seasonal staff. By lowering housing barriers for new hires—many of whom are young workers relocating for hospitality roles—and coordinating with community landlords, this employer-assisted housing supports recruitment and retention in a tight local rental market.
Solution: Employer-Community Housing Partnerships: Coordinate between local employers, chambers of commerce and community groups to develop employer-assisted housing (rent guarantees, down-payment support, dedicated rental blocks) targeted at recruiting and retaining young workers.

Program: Halifax Modular Supportive Housing – Chain Lake Site
Organization: Out of the Cold Community Association (operating for Halifax Regional Municipality)
Description: Halifax Regional Municipality partnered with Out of the Cold Community Association to deploy modular, tiny-home–style units as transitional housing at the Chain Lake Drive site. The village of prefabricated units provides private sleeping spaces with shared supports, creating a rapid, pop-up community that gives people (including younger residents starting work or returning to the city) stable housing while longer-term supply is built.
Solution: Pop-up and Tiny Home Transitional Housing: Organize temporary tiny-home villages or repurpose modular units on community-owned sites to provide transitional housing for young people moving back or starting careers while permanent supply is developed.
Address: 61 Chain Lake Drive, Halifax, NS B3S 1A9

Description: Halifax Partnership regularly hosts employer-education roundtables that gather local companies, universities, NSCC, and training providers to surface real-time skill gaps and coordinate responses. These sessions inform curriculum tweaks, help partners stand up targeted micro-credentials, and secure employer commitments for internships, co-ops, and entry-level roles; the Partnership publishes labour market insights and meeting takeaways that education partners use to adjust programming.
Solution: Community Employer-Education Roundtables: Regular local roundtables where employers, high schools, community colleges, universities, and training providers map current and emerging skill needs, co-design curricula, and commit to concrete co-op/apprenticeship slots. The community organizes and documents outcomes so training aligns to local demand.
Address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1100, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

Description: Techsploration connects female and gender-diverse students in grades 9–12 with women role models working in skilled trades, engineering, and technology across Nova Scotia. Through workplace tours, dedicated job shadowing days, and hands-on team projects guided by volunteer mentors, participants gain career awareness, develop communication and teamwork skills, and build direct connections with potential employers—closely aligning youth learning with real industry needs.
Solution: Youth Career Mentorship Network: A volunteer-based network linking local professionals and tradespeople with young people for short-term job shadowing, project mentorship, and mock workplace projects — improving career awareness and soft skills while building employer connections.
Address: 100 Ilsley Avenue, Unit 110, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1L3

Description: SuperNOVA at Dalhousie University delivers mobile STEM programs—such as coding, robotics, and digital design—by bringing equipment, instructors, and pop-up labs to rural schools and community venues across Nova Scotia. These short, hands-on workshops build foundational tech skills aligned with emerging workforce needs and help bridge school-to-work pathways by exposing youth to practical, in-demand competencies.
Solution: Mobile Training and Maker Labs: A traveling training unit or pop-up maker lab that brings hands-on, short-term training (e.g., welding, coding bootcamps, digital media) to rural communities, lowering barriers to accessing in-demand skills nearby.

Program: Halifax Partnership Labour Market Dashboard and Halifax Index
Description: Halifax Partnership publishes real-time labour market dashboards and the annual Halifax Index, tracking job postings by occupation and skills, labour force trends, and longer-term demographic and industry forecasts for the Halifax region. These insights are used by employers, post-secondary institutions, and training providers to target priority skills and adjust programs, guiding students and job seekers toward areas of current and projected demand.
Solution: Community Skills Forecast and Vacancy Board: A publicly accessible local dashboard maintained by community partners showing short-term and long-term employer needs, projected vacancies, and priority skills — used to guide training providers and student choices.
Address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

Program: Ski Cape Smokey Winter Experience Packages
Description: Ski Cape Smokey coordinates lift tickets, gondola rides, equipment rentals, lessons, and guided snowshoe experiences with partner restaurants and accommodations on the Cabot Trail to create bundled winter getaways. These packages promote multi-operator itineraries during the island’s off-season, increasing visitor length of stay and spend across local businesses. The model extends tourism revenues and winter staffing beyond the traditional summer peak in rural Cape Breton.
Solution: Off-season tourism cooperatives and experience packages: Coordinate tourism operators to offer bundled off-season experiences (food trails, workshops, adventure weekends) to smooth seasonal employment and extend revenues.
Address: 38696 Cabot Trail, Ingonish Beach, NS B0C 1L0

Program: Authentic Seacoast Off-Season Getaways (Distillery, Brewery & Inn Packages)
Description: Authentic Seacoast bundles accommodation at DesBarres Manor Inn with tours and tastings at its craft distillery and brewery, culinary experiences, and guided outdoor activities in and around Guysborough. By coordinating multiple experiences and partners, it offers curated shoulder- and winter-season packages that bring visitors to a rural community outside Halifax. This integrated approach smooths seasonality and sustains local employment across hospitality and craft producers.
Solution: Off-season tourism cooperatives and experience packages: Coordinate tourism operators to offer bundled off-season experiences (food trails, workshops, adventure weekends) to smooth seasonal employment and extend revenues.

Description: Shannex’s CCA Sponsorship Program hires candidates into paid trainee roles and covers tuition and program fees for accredited Continuing Care Assistant education at local colleges. The employer-paid training, guaranteed employment upon graduation, and flexible scheduling during academic terms reduce financial pressure and student debt for early‑career workers, directly aligning with tuition reimbursement and flexible hiring to keep talent in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Local Employer Tuition Reimbursement and Flexible Hiring: Encourage area employers to offer tuition reimbursement, continuing education stipends, and flexible schedules for early-career workers, reducing pressure to leave for higher pay elsewhere.
Address: 1344 Summer Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3H 0A8

Organization: Ronald McDonald House Charities Atlantic in partnership with IWK Health
Description: Staffed by trained volunteers, the IWK Family Room provides short-notice, supervised child-minding and respite support for families at the hospital, including evenings and weekends. This vetted volunteer network offers safe, temporary babysitting for siblings and children so parents can attend urgent appointments or care for hospitalized family members.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Volunteer and Emergency Babysitting Network: A vetted community roster of trained volunteers and peer babysitters who can provide short-notice, evenings or weekend coverage for parents in need.
Address: IWK Health Centre, 5850 University Avenue, Halifax, NS B3K 6R8

Description: Digital Nova Scotia convenes HR and People leaders from member tech companies in an ongoing peer group to exchange policies and templates for flexible work, including compressed workweeks, core-hours frameworks, and hybrid/remote arrangements. Through the peer group and its DigiPort resources, employers co-develop and implement mental‑health benefits and leave policies, helping reduce burnout and strengthen retention of young tech talent across Nova Scotia.
Solution: Employer coalitions promoting flexible work and leave: Local businesses form coalitions to share best practices and jointly offer flexible schedules, compressed workweeks, and mental-health leave policies that reduce burnout and improve retention of young workers.
Address: 7071 Bayers Road, Suite 309, Halifax, NS B3L 2C2

Description: Community Wheels is a non-profit community transit service providing pre-booked, wheelchair-accessible, door-to-door transportation throughout East Hants. Funded through a mix of fares, community fundraising, and government support, it removes transportation barriers for people with disabilities, enabling access to jobs, health care, and social activities in rural areas.
Solution: Accessibility Upgrades and Accessible Transit Initiatives: Mobilize community fundraising and municipal advocacy to improve physical accessibility in public spaces and increase affordable, accessible transit options so people with disabilities can fully participate in work and community life.

Description: Dalhousie’s rideshare platform matches students, staff, and their partners for carpools, reducing commuting time and cost while expanding access to job sites, classes, and childcare across HRM. By coordinating shared rides and offering commuter tools through the Office of Sustainability, the program removes transportation barriers that often deter young families from staying in the region.
Challenge: Retention of Students, Graduates, and Newcomers
Solution: Community Childcare & Transit Solutions: Locally organized childcare co-ops, employer-subsidized spots and ride-share networks that remove practical barriers to employment for young families and partners.

Program: The PIER Community Events & Demo Days
Organization: The PIER at the Halifax Seaport
Description: The PIER at the Halifax Seaport runs industry meetups, member demo days, and knowledge-sharing sessions focused on supply chain, logistics, and ocean innovation. By gathering startups, corporates, students, and remote workers in a living-lab environment, these events foster collaborations and make local career pathways more visible.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Local Networking & Industry Nights: Host regular sector-specific meetups, hackathons and demo nights that bring employers, students and remote workers together to build professional networks and visible career opportunities.

Program: Equity & Access in the Arts Program
Description: Arts Nova Scotia’s Equity & Access in the Arts provides small, flexible project grants to artists and collectives from communities facing barriers (including Indigenous, African Nova Scotian/Black, racialized, Deaf, disabled, and 2SLGBTQIA+ artists). It offers streamlined applications and quick turnaround funding that can cover materials, short-term venue rental, and promotion, directly aligning with a microgrant model that prioritizes underrepresented creators.
Challenge: Support for Arts, Culture, and Creative Industries
Solution: Community Arts Microgrant Program: Create a locally administered microgrant fund (seeded by municipality, businesses, and donors) that awards small, quick-turnaround grants to individual artists, collectives, and pop-up projects to cover materials, short-term venue rental, or promotion. Prioritize youth-led and underrepresented creators and simplify application and reporting requirements.
Address: 1741 Brunswick Street, 3rd Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 3X8

Description: The Canadian Red Cross ERT program recruits and trains local volunteers across Nova Scotia in disaster response, including first aid, shelter/reception centre operations, logistics, and emergency social services. During floods, storms, and wildfires, ERT volunteers assist municipalities with sandbagging, evacuations, and incident coordination at community sites—accelerating on-the-ground response while strengthening neighbourhood ties through volunteer engagement and preparedness workshops.
Solution: Community emergency response teams (CERT): Train local volunteers in search-and-rescue, first aid, sandbagging and incident coordination so neighbourhoods can respond faster during storms and wildfires while building social cohesion.

Description: Halifax Partnership leads a five-year, community-driven plan for inclusive growth that sets measurable targets for talent attraction and retention (including youth and recent graduates), skills development, entrepreneurship, and quality-of-life improvements. The plan includes annual scorecards and check-in milestones with cross-sector partners (municipal, provincial, post-secondary, and industry) to extend planning beyond election cycles and maintain continuity across governments.
Solution: Multi-Year Community Development Plans: Develop 3–5 year plans led by communities that set measurable goals for youth retention, skills development, and quality-of-life improvements; these plans include check-in milestones to extend planning horizons beyond election cycles and create continuity across governments.
Address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

Program: Halifax Index (Interactive Economic and Community Dashboard)
Description: The Halifax Index is an annual, interactive dashboard that consolidates data on labour markets (including youth employment), population, business growth, housing and real estate, transportation, and quality of life. Produced by Halifax Partnership, it enables the public and decision-makers to track performance over time and benchmark Halifax against peer cities, with downloadable data and clear visualizations. By presenting comparable, citywide indicators in one place, it supports data-driven...
Solution: Community Performance Dashboards: Publish simple, accessible dashboards tracking key local indicators (jobs for youth, housing availability, transit access, program take-up) so residents and officials can see progress, compare neighbourhoods, and make data-driven choices.
Address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1201, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

Organization: St. Margaret’s Bay Community Transportation Society
Description: Community Wheels is a volunteer-driven, door-to-door community transit service serving the rural St. Margaret’s Bay area. Riders can pre-book subsidized trips for medical, shopping, and social/recreational activities, including evening events, and drivers provide door-to-door assistance that functions as a safe escort for seniors and youth. By filling gaps in limited public transit after hours, it enables residents to attend community programming and reduces isolation in smaller communities.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Community transportation for evening events: Coordinate volunteer-run or subsidized shuttle services and safe-route escorts for teens and seniors to access evening programming, increasing attendance and reducing barriers created by limited transit in smaller towns.
Address: 5288 St. Margarets Bay Road, Upper Tantallon, NS B3Z 2H3

Program: Board Game Night & Makerspace Drop-ins (Kentville Public Library)
Description: Kentville Public Library offers recurring Board Game Nights, craft circles, and maker-style drop-ins that invite families, teens, working adults, and older adults to create, play, and learn together. These intergenerational clubs and social evenings are free or low-cost and designed to be welcoming for all ages, building a reliable third-place routine in the town core. The hands-on, collaborative format supports casual mentorship and neighborly connections across generations.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Intergenerational clubs and regular social nights: Create recurring clubs (game nights, maker nights, storytelling, music) that intentionally mix youth, working-age adults and seniors to strengthen social ties and create reliable third-place routines.

Program: Port Days Community Open House and Tours
Description: During Port Days and related open-house programming, the Halifax Port Authority offers guided tours and public events that bring residents onto port properties to meet terminal operators, logistics firms, and marine service providers. By opening these workplaces and explaining operations firsthand, the port demystifies career paths and highlights the global opportunities and quality of life connected to Halifax’s working waterfront.
Solution: Neighbourhood Open Homes and Employer Tours: Host regular open-house events where residents tour workplaces, co-working spaces, maker spaces and sample neighborhoods to experience local workplaces and lifestyle firsthand, dismantling misconceptions through direct exposure.

Description: Feed Nova Scotia works directly with Nova Scotia farmers and producers to collect surplus and donated crops—including post-harvest and seasonal excess—and moves that fresh produce through a province-wide network of community food banks, meal programs, and shelters. By coordinating farm partnerships and food rescue (including field gleaning when possible), they increase access to healthy fruits and vegetables at neighborhood hubs and help households reduce grocery costs.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Gardens, Gleaning Networks and Farm Partnerships: Neighbourhood gardens on municipal or church land, paired with gleaning programs that collect surplus from local farms and distribute it through community hubs, increasing access to fresh produce and reducing grocery bills.

Description: Feed Nova Scotia’s advocacy program compiles data and stories from people accessing food support across the province to highlight how food, transportation, and utility costs strain household budgets. Using this lived‑experience evidence, they engage municipal and provincial leaders to push for income‑based solutions—like living‑wage policies, stronger income assistance, and affordable access programs—that reduce cost‑of‑living pressures beyond housing.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Advocacy Network for Local Cost-of-Living Policies: A community-led coalition that collects lived-experience data and advocates municipal/provincial leaders for targeted supports (transit passes, childcare subsidies, living-wage bylaws), amplifying community-driven policy wins.

Description: Nova Scotia Community College engages carpentry, electrical, and related trades students in building modular or panelized small homes and tiny homes as applied learning projects with municipalities and non-profits across the province. These collaborations pilot fast, lower-cost prefabricated units that can be placed on community or institutional land as affordable or supportive rentals, adding supply while training local talent and supporting the regional construction workforce.
Solution: Modular/Prefab Pilot Projects: Partner with local builders and trades training programs to pilot modular or prefabricated homes on community land or church lots — faster, cheaper rental units that also create local jobs.

Description: Nova Scotia Community College convenes Program Advisory Committees for nearly every program, bringing together local employers, faculty, high schools, and training partners to map current and emerging skill needs. These roundtables co-design and update curricula, identify equipment/technology requirements, and secure co-op and work-integrated learning placements; outcomes are documented and feed directly into program revisions so training aligns to regional labour market demand.
Solution: Community Employer-Education Roundtables: Regular local roundtables where employers, high schools, community colleges, universities, and training providers map current and emerging skill needs, co-design curricula, and commit to concrete co-op/apprenticeship slots. The community organizes and documents outcomes so training aligns to local demand.

Description: NSCC runs ongoing RPL information sessions, portfolio workshops, challenge exams, and skills demonstrations that grant credit for informal and work-based learning. By converting prior experience into course credit and advanced standing recognized by local employers, NSCC shortens training time and speeds transitions into co-ops, apprenticeships, and jobs across Nova Scotia.
Solution: Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) Clinics: Community centers offering regular RPL workshops and assessment days to help young people and newcomers convert informal, volunteer, or on-the-job experience into recognized credentials that local employers accept.

Program: NSCC Industry-Partnered Capstone and Applied Research Projects
Description: Nova Scotia Community College integrates employer-sponsored capstone and applied research projects into diploma and degree programs, where student teams deliver real solutions for local businesses and non-profits. These projects are assessed for academic credit and are scoped with industry partners, aligning curriculum with current labour market needs while giving learners tangible, portfolio-ready experience.
Solution: School-Enterprise Project Partnerships: Programs where schools partner with local businesses and non-profits on real projects (product design, service delivery, community events) that count for credit and provide tangible experience employers value.

Program: Financial Aid & Awards: Financial Literacy Workshops and Advising
Description: NSCC offers campus-based and virtual financial literacy sessions on budgeting, credit, responsible borrowing, and post-graduation loan repayment. Learners can access one-on-one advising to map out repayment timelines, apply for the Repayment Assistance Plan or grants/forgiveness where eligible, and consider consolidation or refinancing options to reduce long-term debt pressure.
Solution: Financial Literacy, Debt Counseling and Repayment Clinics: Host regular community workshops and one-on-one clinics on budgeting, loan repayment strategies, refinancing, and accessing forgiveness programs to reduce long-term debt burdens.

Program: NSCC Open House and Trades & Technology Showcases
Description: Nova Scotia Community College hosts campus open houses and shop tours where instructors, apprentices, and employer partners present skilled trades, construction, and technology programs. Participants explore labs, hear alumni stories, and learn about wages, credentials, and apprenticeship pathways—functioning as local job showcases and employer-connected open-house events that elevate pride in trades careers.
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: Local Career Awareness Campaigns: Run community storytelling, job showcases, and employer open-house events highlighting career paths, earnings, and pride in local trades, care work, and construction.

Description: IGNITE’s Mobile Innovation Lab is a traveling makerspace that brings 3D printers, robotics kits, VR/AR gear, and prototyping tools to rural communities on a rotating schedule. The unit sets up pop-up labs in schools, community centres, and Indigenous communities to deliver hands-on tech and entrepreneurship workshops that align with local employer and industry needs.
Solution: Mobile Training Units and Pop-up Labs for Rural Areas: Equipped trailers or temporary pop-up labs that bring hands-on trade, tech and green-skills training to small towns and Indigenous communities on a rotating schedule.
Address: 610 East River Road, Suite 150, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3S2

Description: IGNITE Atlantic runs practical clinics, office hours, and workshops that guide local shops, trades and artists through standing up e-commerce sites, configuring digital payments and POS, and adopting online booking and collaboration tools. Their teams in Western and Northern Nova Scotia deliver tailored, step-by-step support—often in partnership with local stakeholders—to help rural entrepreneurs translate better broadband into online sales, remote client services, and streamlined digital wor...
Solution: Local Business Digitalization and E‑commerce Clinics: Provide tailored support for local shops, trades and artists to establish online storefronts, digital payment systems and remote-client workflows so improved internet directly boosts local economic opportunities.

Description: IGNITE Atlantic hosts free expert office hours and themed clinics where local lawyers, accountants, and marketers volunteer their time to advise rural founders. Entrepreneurs receive hands‑on help with incorporation and contracts, bookkeeping setup and tax basics, and practical guidance for navigating government procurement and tendering processes.
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Volunteer Professional Clinics: Local lawyers, accountants and marketers provide pro-bono clinics and office hours to help founders with incorporation, contracts, bookkeeping and tendering at no or low cost.

Description: IGNITE Atlantic operates rural innovation hubs that connect youth, students, and founders with local mentors, Entrepreneurs-in-Residence, and industry partners in Nova Scotia. Through office hours, workshops, and project-based collaborations, participants receive practical advice, introductions to employers, and pathways to placements with local companies. The program builds long-term relationships between emerging talent and community-based entrepreneurs, anchoring careers and startups in th...
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Local Mentorship & Alumni Networks: Create community-run mentorship programs that connect young people with local alumni, tradespeople, entrepreneurs and professionals for career advice, internships, and long-term relationships that strengthen personal ties to the region.
Address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

Program: IGNITE Atlantic Startup Showcase & Community Pop-Ups
Description: IGNITE Atlantic runs recurring showcases, pitch nights, and pop-up markets in rural communities where startups, student teams, and makers present products and prototypes to the public. Employers, mentors, and investors attend to network and recruit, turning innovation into a celebratory, community-facing experience that spotlights opportunity in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Community Festivals that Showcase Opportunity: Build festivals or pop-up markets focused on local innovation, trades, arts and food where young people can exhibit projects, entrepreneurs can pitch ideas and employers can recruit, making opportunity visible and celebratory.
Address: 352 East River Road, New Glasgow, NS B2H 3P7

Description: HRM’s Youth Advisory Committee engages young residents to provide recommendations to Regional Council on policies that affect them, including housing and planning matters. YAC members participate in consultations and hearings to champion faster approvals for gentle infill, affordability measures such as inclusionary policies, and incentives for small rental units—ensuring youth voices inform council decisions.
Solution: Community Advocacy for Faster Approvals and Inclusionary Policies: Mobilize neighborhood associations, businesses and youth groups to advocate at council for faster permitting for modest infill, inclusionary zoning on new developments, and incentives for small-scale rental projects.

Description: Halifax Regional Municipality requires short-term rental operators to register and complies with provincial tourist accommodation registration, while restricting entire-home short-term rentals to primary residences in most residential zones. This creates a transparent, local registry of units being used as short-term rentals and enables targeted enforcement to reduce commercial STRs, helping shift vacant or underused dwellings back into the long-term rental market.
Solution: Community Vacancy Registry and Vacancy Tax Advocacy: Collect local data on vacant units through a community registry and campaign for municipal vacancy taxes or incentives to bring units back into the rental market.

Program: Municipal Access Agreements (MAA) and Utility Right‑of‑Way Permitting
Description: Halifax Regional Municipality administers Municipal Access Agreements and right‑of‑way permits that allow telecommunications providers to occupy municipal corridors and, where available, municipal duct banks. The standardized agreements coordinate with other utilities and city departments so multiple providers can share corridors, poles, and conduit routes with consistent technical and restoration requirements. By reducing duplication and clarifying access terms, the MAA framework supports co...
Solution: Shared Infrastructure Agreements (Poles, Conduits and Towers): Coordinate municipalities, utilities and landowners to enable shared access to poles, conduits and tower sites. Community groups can broker or manage agreements so multiple providers can cost-effectively extend service into rural areas.

Program: Backyard Suites (Accessory Dwelling Units) – Standardized Design and Permit Package
Description: HRM’s Backyard Suites program provides a standardized application package with typical drawings, siting rules, and design criteria that allow repeatable, code‑compliant ADU layouts to be reviewed and approved more quickly. By publishing consistent templates and accepted design parameters across the municipality, it operationalizes a pre‑approved approach that reduces friction for accessory units and accelerates permit turnaround for common designs.
Solution: Pre‑Approved Local Design Library: Develop a set of common, pre‑approved designs for tiny homes, accessory units, renewable installations and small commercial fitouts that municipalities can endorse to speed approvals for repeatable projects.

Program: Halifax Housing Accelerator Fund – Fast-Track Development Approvals
Description: Under its Housing Accelerator Fund action plan, HRM is piloting faster, clearer approvals through measures like pre-approved designs (e.g., accessory/backyard suites), published checklists, digital permitting, and prioritized review lanes for affordable and modular projects. These steps reduce permitting friction, establish guaranteed timelines, and create a repeatable, low-risk pathway for multi-site housing pilots to scale.
Solution: Local Fast‑Track Pilot Projects: Organize community-backed pilot projects (e.g., a cluster of modular homes or community solar) and negotiate a municipal fast‑track review and clear checklist to prove a repeatable, low‑risk approval path.

Program: Homelessness in the Halifax Region Data Dashboard
Description: HRM publishes regularly updated statistics on homelessness, including by-name list trends, shelter occupancy, and housing placements, using local, community-collected data through coordinated access and HIFIS. By making these metrics public, the dashboard functions as a community scorecard that drives transparency and accountability across municipal, provincial, and community partners working to improve equitable access to housing and services.
Solution: Data, Accountability and Community Dashboard: Collect disaggregated local data (voluntary and community governed) on employment, education, housing and service access; publish a regular public dashboard and community scorecard to track progress and hold institutions accountable.

Program: Saint Mary’s Boat Club Living Shoreline
Description: Halifax Regional Municipality replaced a deteriorating seawall at the Saint Mary’s Boat Club on the Northwest Arm with a living shoreline that uses rock sills, coir logs, and native salt-marsh vegetation to reduce wave energy, control erosion, and improve intertidal habitat. The site serves as a public demonstration of nature-based coastal protection and involves local stewardship and seasonal maintenance and monitoring activities.
Solution: Living shorelines and salt-marsh restoration: Community-led projects to restore marshes, eelgrass beds, and create living shorelines that absorb wave energy and reduce erosion, protecting homes and fisheries while providing local stewardship and seasonal jobs.

Program: Green Network Plan – Land Acquisition for Coastal and Flood Resilience
Description: HRM’s Green Network Plan guides targeted, voluntary land acquisition and easements in areas that provide climate resilience, including floodplains, riparian corridors, and vulnerable coasts. By purchasing at-risk parcels or accepting dedications and converting them to parks, trails, and natural buffers, HRM implements a form of managed retreat that limits redevelopment in hazard-prone locations and creates public green space that absorbs storm surge and overland flooding.
Solution: Planned buyouts and voluntary managed retreat program: A locally managed, transparent program offering fair purchase or relocation support for repeatedly damaged properties, converting vulnerable land to public green space or coastal buffers.

Program: Centre Plan Key Performance Indicator (KPI) Dashboard
Description: Halifax Regional Municipality publishes an online KPI dashboard that tracks development activity, new housing units, density targets, and related planning indicators across the Regional Centre. The dashboard lets residents, councillors, and planners monitor progress by area, compare trends across neighbourhoods, and assess the take-up of planning tools to guide housing and infrastructure decisions. This accessible, regularly updated view supports coordinated, evidence-based choices across mun...
Solution: Community Performance Dashboards: Publish simple, accessible dashboards tracking key local indicators (jobs for youth, housing availability, transit access, program take-up) so residents and officials can see progress, compare neighbourhoods, and make data-driven choices.

Description: Halifax Regional Municipality redesigned Argyle and Grafton Streets into a pedestrian‑priority public space with integrated seating, widened sidewalks, programmable and safety lighting, bike racks, and power for events—supporting nightlife and all‑season use. The streetscape creates a welcoming, flexible ‘third place’ that encourages social connection and activity in the downtown core.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Install lighting, seating and Wi‑Fi in public spaces: Small capital projects—better lighting, weatherproof seating, bike racks, and public Wi‑Fi—make plazas and waterfronts comfortable and safe for longer use. Local groups can lead fundraising and adopt-a-space maintenance.

Program: Mi’kmaw Native Friendship Centre – Cultural, Language, and Healing Programs
Description: An Indigenous-led urban service hub that co-designs programs with Mi’kmaq Elders and community members, the Centre delivers Mi’kmaw language classes, cultural workshops, and land-based activities that strengthen identity and belonging. It partners with health, housing, and justice agencies to ensure culturally safe, Indigenous-governed services—such as healing circles and wraparound supports—are delivered to urban Indigenous peoples and allies in Halifax.
Solution: Indigenous-Led Partnerships and Cultural Revitalization: Partner with Mi’kmaq communities to co-design programs, support language and cultural revitalization projects, host jointly governed healing circles, and ensure Indigenous leadership in service delivery affecting their communities.

Program: Perennia Collaborative Applied Research and Extension Programs
Description: Perennia convenes producers, processors, municipalities, Dalhousie’s Faculty of Agriculture, and provincial/federal funders (e.g., Sustainable Canadian Agricultural Partnership) to pool matching funds for applied research, extension, and pilot projects in agri-food. These consortia-based initiatives operate across rural regions of Nova Scotia, reduce duplication among jurisdictions, and sustain multi-year projects that help align policy, market needs, and community outcomes.
Solution: Joint Funding Consortia: Build coalitions of municipalities, non-profits, businesses, and post-secondary institutions that pool grant-matching funds to co-invest in cross-jurisdictional projects, making it easier to pursue longer-term initiatives that transcend political cycles.
Address: 199 Innovation Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2H5

Description: EAC’s Built Environment work mobilizes residents and partners to support compact, transit‑oriented communities, advocating for inclusionary housing tools, density bonuses, and parking reform in municipal plans. The team organizes campaigns, produces policy briefs, and collaborates with municipalities to remove zoning barriers and increase affordable housing near services and frequent transit.
Solution: Inclusionary Zoning and Planning Advocacy: Organize community campaigns to work with municipalities to adopt inclusionary zoning, density bonuses and reduced parking rules to increase the supply of affordable units near services and transit.

Description: Ecology Action Centre trains community volunteers, local organizations, and municipal partners to collect standardized water quality and habitat data in watersheds and along the coast across Nova Scotia. They curate and interpret these community-level datasets, publish accessible reports, and translate findings into briefs and submissions to municipal, provincial, and federal policymakers—shrinking data gaps and ensuring locally gathered evidence informs higher-level decisions.
Solution: Community Data Stewards Program: Train volunteers and staff from local organizations to collect, curate, and interpret community-level data (surveys, vacancy rates, youth employment outcomes) so data gaps shrink and local evidence feeds into higher-level policy conversations.

Program: Powerline Technician Apprenticeship and Grid Operations Training
Description: Nova Scotia Power recruits and trains Powerline Technician (PLT) apprentices and substation technicians to build, maintain, and modernize the provincial grid, including hands-on training with live-line tools, distribution equipment, and substations. The utility also provides in-house training for system/dispatch operators on SCADA and protection-and-control systems, developing local control‑system operators who can integrate renewables and manage reliability. The programs are delivered in par...
Challenge: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth
Solution: Local Workforce Training and Apprenticeship Programs: Partner with colleges, unions and employers to create fast‑track training for grid technicians, solar installers, battery specialists and control‑system operators to ensure skilled local labour for growth.
Address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Description: Build Nova Scotia coordinates the rapid deployment of modular, prefabricated supportive housing on provincially or municipally owned community lands in the Halifax Region. By procuring modular units and contracting local builders and trades for site servicing and assembly, the initiative delivers rental units much faster and at lower cost while creating local construction jobs and adding urgently needed supply.
Solution: Modular/Prefab Pilot Projects: Partner with local builders and trades training programs to pilot modular or prefabricated homes on community land or church lots — faster, cheaper rental units that also create local jobs.
Address: 1875 Upper Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 1S9

Description: Build Nova Scotia leads a province-wide program to identify cellular coverage gaps and deploy solutions such as small cells and signal boosters on community-owned and public assets (e.g., community halls, fire stations, water towers, and municipal buildings). The program coordinates permitting, access to sites, and cost-sharing through public–private partnerships with carriers and integrators to improve mobile service in rural and underserved areas.

Program: Salt Yard and Salt Yard Too Pop-Up Retail (Halifax Waterfront)
Description: Build Nova Scotia curates seasonal pop-up retail kiosks and container shops along the Halifax Waterfront, offering short-term, low-cost licenses to rotating local makers, food startups, and artists. The program provides turnkey, high-foot-traffic stalls without long-term leases, enabling entrepreneurs to test products, validate demand, and gain exposure in a shared retail environment.

In tandem with its waterfront stewardship, the organization also invests in public-realm upgrades—weather‑resistant seating, lighting, bike racks, and power—making plazas and boardwalks comfortable, safe, and usable for longer hours and seasons.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Install lighting, seating and Wi‑Fi in public spaces: Small capital projects—better lighting, weatherproof seating, bike racks, and public Wi‑Fi—make plazas and waterfronts comfortable and safe for longer use. Local groups can lead fundraising and adopt-a-space maintenance.

Description: Volta hosts recurring, facilitated peer-to-peer groups for startup leaders (e.g., founders, CTOs, marketers) where experienced operators and mentors guide discussions on current business bottlenecks. Participants workshop live issues, exchange playbooks, and set action items, creating peer accountability and practical problem solving within a trusted circle.
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Mentorship Circles and Peer Learning Groups: Organize regular, facilitated mentorship circles pairing experienced local business owners with new entrepreneurs for skill-building, peer accountability and practical problem solving.

Description: Volta hosts frequent tech-community meetups, socials, talks, and student-focused events (e.g., founder meetups, Women in Tech gatherings, lunch-and-learns) that welcome students, newcomers, and professionals. These interest-based circles help people plug into Halifax’s innovation community quickly, building cross-cultural networks that make the region stickier for emerging talent.
Challenge: Retention of Students, Graduates, and Newcomers

Description: Volta invites students, newcomers, and residents to tour its downtown startup hub, with regular open houses and bookable tours that take visitors through co-working floors, startup offices, and community event spaces. Address: 358 Herring Cove Road, Suite 100, Halifax, NS B3R 1V8

Description: YWCA Halifax brings together families, early childhood educators, women’s organizations, and local employers to advocate to the Province of Nova Scotia for sustainable operating funding, fair wages for ECEs, and child-care models that include flexible and after-hours care. Description: Halifax Public Libraries provides in-branch community notice boards and community spaces that families and local caregivers use to post and respond to nanny-share and babysitting opportunities. Solution: Shared Caregiver Pooling Platform: A community app or bulletin board that helps parents coordinate shifts, share caregivers or form micro-pods with transparent scheduling and micro-payments.

Program: Community Wellness and Job Resource Fairs
Description: Halifax Public Libraries regularly hosts community fairs at branches like the Central Library that bring together mental‑health providers, employment counsellors, and local employers in one accessible venue. Solution: Time Banks and Skill-Swap Platforms: Local time-banking systems where residents exchange hours of work (childcare, tutoring, repairs) instead of money, building mutual aid networks that cut service costs for young people.

Description: The Town of Lunenburg designates the Lunenburg Community Centre as an emergency warming/comfort centre, leveraging backup power, public WiFi, showers, and kitchen facilities to support residents during storms and extended outages. Solution: Neighborhood Densification Charrettes and Design Guides: Host local design charrettes to identify low-impact densification opportunities (laneway homes, triplexes) and produce community-backed design guides to speed approvals and reduce NIMBY resistance.

Description: Through the Plan Wolfville process, the Town held public design workshops/charrettes to identify where and how gentle density—such as accessory/secondary suites, small multiplexes and townhouses—could fit within existing neighbourhoods. The resulting policies and Core Area architectural/design guidelines provide clear, pre-approved forms and infill standards that streamline approvals and address neighbourhood concerns with community-vetted solutions.
Solution: Neighborhood Densification Charrettes and Design Guides: Host local design charrettes to identify low-impact densification opportunities (laneway homes, triplexes) and produce community-backed design guides to speed approvals and reduce NIMBY resistance.
