Program: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia — Volunteer Build Program
Description: Habitat for Humanity Nova Scotia organizes volunteer build crews—often including trades students from NSCC and local universities—who work alongside experienced staff and trades professionals to construct and, when suitable, rehabilitate homes. By leveraging community volunteers and student placements, the program increases the supply of safe, energy‑efficient, entry-level affordable homes for families across the province. These supervised builds and rehabs both expand affordable housing stoc...
Solution: Volunteer Rehab and Skills-Training Crews: Create volunteer teams combining trades students and community volunteers to renovate vacant or substandard units, pairing skill-building opportunities with increases in safe, affordable housing stock.

Program: Matched Savings and Financial Empowerment Programs
Description: YWCA Halifax runs group-based financial empowerment and matched-savings initiatives that help women and gender-diverse participants set savings goals, build peer support, and receive matched funds for education, training, or employment needs. These programs function as cooperative savings models, enabling participants to accumulate small savings and access low- or no-cost funds for tuition, certification, or emergencies in place of high-interest credit.
Solution: Peer Savings Groups and Cooperative Finance Models: Promote rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCA), cooperative banking products, and credit-union partnerships that enable small-scale savings and emergency lending without high interest.
Address: 358 Herring Cove Road, Halifax, NS B3R 1V8

Organization: Cape Breton Family Place Resource Centre
Description: Family Place offers free parent programs, workshops, and employment supports with on‑site childminding and early learning. Many activities are supported by older adult volunteers and retired caregivers who provide warm, supervised engagement for children, creating intergenerational care that enables parents—especially newcomers and single parents—to attend classes, appointments, or work‑search activities.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Intergenerational Care Programs: Match seniors and older volunteers with families so seniors provide part-time supervised care and engagement, offering companionship for elders and reliable support for parents.

Program: Truro Business Parks (Truro Business Park and Truro Industrial Park)
Description: The Town of Truro offers serviced, pre‑zoned lots in its business parks, with established development standards and as‑of‑right permissions that minimize the need for rezonings or development agreements. By banking and preparing land in advance, the program shortens approval timelines and reduces costs for startups and growing companies.
Solution: Pre‑Zoned Community Land Bank: Create a community land trust that acquires and holds lots pre‑zoned for affordable housing, small businesses or renewable installations, reducing time spent rezoning and permitting.

Description: The Town of Truro maintains Salmon River floodplain maps and an online viewer and augments them with resident-reported flooding hotspots gathered through public meetings and service requests to identify high‑risk streets, basements, and access routes. The Town provides printed and online homeowner guides, development checklists, and emergency detour information so residents, prospective homebuyers, and insurers can assess parcel‑level flood risk and understand mitigation and adaptation measures.
Solution: Community flood mapping and risk communication: Volunteer-driven mapping of high-risk streets, basements and access routes combined with clear, locally distributed guidance so residents, prospective homebuyers and insurers understand true risk and adaptation options.

Description: The Town of Truro operates a local monitoring network with river stage gauges on the Salmon River and shares real-time levels and flood risk updates through public web dashboards and alerts. This open data helps residents prepare for flood events and supports municipal planning and infrastructure decisions, reducing risk in a community highly exposed to storm-driven flooding.
Solution: Local monitoring network and data sharing: Volunteer-operated sensors and shoreline change monitoring with open data dashboards to inform local planning, insurance underwriting and timely warnings for residents.

Description: Truro’s four-year strategic plan establishes measurable objectives for workforce and population growth, downtown revitalization, active transportation, recreation, and service improvements that directly support youth retention and quality of life. The town conducts regular progress updates and collaborates with regional partners (e.g., County of Colchester, post-secondary institutions, and the Province) to coordinate implementation beyond election cycles and maintain accountability.
Solution: Multi-Year Community Development Plans: Develop 3–5 year plans led by communities that set measurable goals for youth retention, skills development, and quality-of-life improvements; these plans include check-in milestones to extend planning horizons beyond election cycles and create continuity across governments.

Description: Nova Scotia Health offers bursaries and sponsorships that cover tuition or repay student costs for in‑demand health professions (e.g., medical laboratory technologists, diagnostic imaging, respiratory therapy), tied to signed multi‑year return‑of‑service commitments in the provincial health system. These incentives function as loan‑for‑service supports by offsetting student debt in exchange for working in priority roles and locations.
Solution: Loan-for-Service and Local Loan Forgiveness Programs: Set up community or municipal programs that forgive or repay portions of student debt in exchange for multi-year service in schools, healthcare, emergency services, or other priority local workplaces.

Program: Clinical Learner Travel and Accommodation Support
Description: Nova Scotia Health offers travel and accommodation reimbursements for health‑profession students completing clinical placements in regional and rural facilities across the province. Support helps cover mileage, temporary housing, and transit so learners can train in communities beyond Halifax without personal financial strain. This reduces mobility barriers and encourages youth to pursue in-demand health careers while experiencing opportunities in different Nova Scotia regions.
Solution: Mobility Scholarships and Travel Stipends for Youth: Establish small community funds that provide travel grants or transit subsidies for young people pursuing internships, apprenticeships, or cultural opportunities in other towns — reducing mobility barriers that otherwise force relocation.
Address: 90 Lovett Lake Court, Halifax, NS B3S 0H6

Description: TeleHealthNS provides private, internet-enabled rooms equipped with secure video conferencing so patients can connect with specialists and primary care providers without having to travel long distances. At the Yarmouth Regional Hospital site, hospital staff help patients check in, set up the connection, and ensure clinical peripherals (e.g., digital stethoscopes, cameras) work during the appointment—delivering exactly the kind of assisted telehealth kiosk experience needed in rural areas.
Solution: Telehealth and Remote-Service Kiosks: Set up private, internet-enabled kiosks at clinics, community centres or libraries where residents can connect to telehealth providers, employment services or government portals with on-site assistance as needed.

Program: TeleHealthNS – Inverness Consolidated Memorial Hospital Site
Description: TeleHealthNS operates a dedicated telehealth room at the Inverness Consolidated Memorial Hospital, providing a private, internet-enabled space for patients to connect with distant providers. Clinical and administrative staff offer on-site assistance before and during sessions, effectively delivering a kiosk-style service that bridges broadband and distance barriers in rural Cape Breton.
Solution: Telehealth and Remote-Service Kiosks: Set up private, internet-enabled kiosks at clinics, community centres or libraries where residents can connect to telehealth providers, employment services or government portals with on-site assistance as needed.

Program: Provincial Supply Chain (Procurement) for Health Services
Description: Nova Scotia Health operates a shared provincial supply chain and procurement function that consolidates purchasing for hospitals and health facilities across the province, often coordinating with IWK and group purchasing while also running provincial RFPs and standing offers. By combining the demand of many sites and using regional lots and multi‑year agreements, the program creates predictable institutional contracts that small Nova Scotia suppliers can service without marketing to each faci...
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Local Procurement Consortia: Form buyer consortia of schools, health centres and municipalities to aggregate demand and create predictable contracts that make it easier for small local suppliers to win work.
Address: 90 Lovett Lake Court, Beechville, NS B3T 0H1

Description: NECHC’s social workers and outreach staff help residents—especially marginalized youth, newcomers, and people experiencing homelessness—navigate the health and social service systems. They book primary care and specialist appointments, explain referrals and care plans, support completion of medical and income-support forms, and connect clients to community resources and transportation options to attend care.
Solution: Community health navigator program: Local volunteers and social-service workers help residents—especially youth and newcomers—book appointments, understand referrals, complete intake forms, and connect to community resources and transportation options.

Program: Summer Student Employment (Programs and Community Outreach)
Description: Cape Breton Regional Library employs students in paid positions to deliver children’s reading clubs, digital literacy workshops, community outreach, and local history projects across its branches. Working at the library embeds youth in civic life, builds leadership and service skills, and highlights public-sector and cultural careers that contribute directly to community well-being.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Civic Learning & Community Service Pathways: Create paid youth positions in municipal projects, cultural organizations and non-profits to build local leadership, deepen civic ties, and demonstrate viable careers that contribute to community life.

Description: Health Association Nova Scotia provides shared recruitment and onboarding services for a consortium of long-term care and home care employers that pool membership resources. The program coordinates province-wide hiring fairs, centralized screening, and standardized training/orientation (e.g., for CCAs) while arranging practical placements across member facilities to accelerate hiring and reduce costs for individual organizations.
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: Employer Training Consortium: Form a cooperative of local employers that pools funds and staff time to run shared training programs, rotating placements, and joint hiring fairs to reduce individual costs.

Description: Nova Scotia Health’s “More Than Medicine” campaign markets the province’s lifestyle, communities, and career growth stories to recruit and retain health professionals, residents, and students. The initiative combines compelling place-based narratives with employer outreach and relocation support, framing Nova Scotia as a rewarding place to build a life and career—directly countering brain drain in a critical sector.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Place-Based Branding & Talent Campaigns: Develop community-led marketing that highlights local quality of life, career success stories and cultural strengths to reframe the region as an attractive long-term home for young people.
Address: 1276 South Park Street, Halifax, NS B3H 2Y9

Program: Early Childhood Education Centre (ECEC) and Community Hub
Description: The North Grove combines a licensed Early Childhood Education Centre with a community hub that offers work-friendly spaces, Wi‑Fi, and program rooms used for employment, training, and entrepreneurship supports. Parents can place their children in affordable, licensed childcare on-site while they work remotely, attend virtual meetings, job search, or join skills programs in the same building—delivering a practical hybrid work hub with childcare that reduces the need to commute or relocate.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Hybrid Work Hubs with Childcare: Combine co-working facilities with affordable childcare and family-friendly hours so young parents can pursue remote or local work without relocating for better services.

Description: Maritime Bus provides chartered coaches and pop-up shuttle services for festivals, tournaments, and seasonal workforce needs across Nova Scotia, creating temporary links between smaller towns and event/job sites. These on-demand, short-term shuttles help organizers move people safely and efficiently while demonstrating intercommunity demand that can inform permanent intercity service planning.
Solution: Pop-up Event and Seasonal Shuttles: Organize temporary shuttles for festivals, market days, and seasonal employment peaks that connect isolated communities to cultural and job opportunities, demonstrating demand and building case studies for permanent services.

Program: Maritime Bus Online Booking and E‑Tickets
Description: Maritime Bus operates the intercity coach network across Nova Scotia and the Maritimes, offering online schedules, mobile-friendly booking, and e‑tickets that simplify longer, multi‑leg travel. By centralizing intercity trip information and fare purchases, it complements local transit and ferry services, helping riders connect rural and urban destinations for work, education, and culture.
Solution: Integrated Mobility Info and Ticketing App: Develop a community-backed transit information portal and ticketing system that aggregates schedules, real-time updates, ride-matching, and fare purchases for shuttles, buses, ferries and microtransit, lowering friction for multi-leg journeys across providers.

Description: Bridgewater’s Diversity and Inclusion Committee is a resident-based advisory body that guides the Town’s Diversity & Inclusion Strategy and action plans. It reviews municipal policies and services for equity impacts, proposes policy improvements to address racism and systemic barriers, partners with local organizations to deliver community education on inclusion and anti-racism, and tracks progress for Council to ensure accountability.
Solution: Community Anti-Racism & Inclusion Task Force: Create a citizen-led task force made up of representatives from Black, Mi’kmaq, newcomer, 2SLGBTQIA+, disability and youth communities to audit local institutions, propose policy changes, coordinate community education, and monitor progress on inclusion goals.

Program: Community Internet Services and Equipment Support
Description: Chebucto Community Net is a non-profit community ISP that aggregates local subscribers to offer low-cost internet plans and provides guidance and access to compatible modems/routers sourced at scale. By coordinating member sign‑ups and facilitating bulk procurement of home connectivity equipment at cost, Chebucto reduces per-household expenses and supports wider adoption of reliable home internet in the Halifax area.
Solution: Bulk Purchasing Programs for Home Connectivity and Devices: Organize cooperative buying programs so households can purchase routers, extenders, antennas or low-cost ISP plans in bulk to lower per-unit costs and speed adoption. Local businesses or the municipality can coordinate procurement and distribution.

Description: Colchester-East Hants Public Library’s Truro Library provides free, reservable study rooms, strong Wi‑Fi, and public computers, creating a private, secure setting for telehealth sessions. Library staff assist with setting up video calls and basic troubleshooting, and the system offers loanable tech (such as hotspots/tablets where available), helping patrons overcome privacy and device barriers to attend virtual medical or counselling appointments.
Solution: Telehealth access hubs in libraries and community centres: Public spaces provide private booths, reliable internet, device loans, and staff assistance so people can attend virtual medical or counselling appointments without technology or privacy barriers.
Address: Truro Public Library, 754 Prince Street, Truro, NS B2N 1G9

Program: Borrow a Wi‑Fi Hub and Tech Help by Appointment
Description: Colchester-East Hants Public Library lends Wi‑Fi hotspot devices and provides one-on-one technology help sessions supported by trained staff and volunteers. Residents can receive step-by-step assistance to connect and secure home networks, set up routers and Wi‑Fi extenders, and troubleshoot connectivity issues, including help getting loaned hotspots working. By pairing connectivity tools with community tech stewards, the library lowers barriers for people with limited technical skills in rur...
Solution: Volunteer Digital Stewards and Installation Teams: Train local volunteers to help neighbours install routers, set up Wi‑Fi extenders, configure secure home networks and maintain local wireless hotspots. This lowers barriers for older residents and those with limited technical skills.

Organization: Municipality of the County of Kings
Description: Kings 2050 is a collaborative planning framework among the Municipality of the County of Kings and the Towns of Kentville, Wolfville, and Berwick to align municipal planning strategies, land-use bylaws, and growth management. The initiative standardizes definitions and development standards and has engaged local business and community associations to streamline permitting, making approvals more predictable and consistent across municipal boundaries in the Valley region.
Solution: Cross‑Municipal Community Coalition: Form a coalition of neighbourhood associations and chambers of commerce across nearby municipalities to jointly advocate for aligned bylaws, standard forms and reciprocal permitting practices.
Address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

Organization: Construction Association of Nova Scotia (with Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency, NSCC, and education partners)
Description: BFY is a province-wide partnership that convenes employers, high schools, the Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency, NSCC, and government to identify construction-sector skill needs and create clear pathways from school to apprenticeship. Through regional planning roundtables, partners align safety and job-readiness training, co-design work experiences, and employers commit to paid summer placements that often transition into apprenticeship; results and student outcomes are tracked to refine trai...
Solution: Community Employer-Education Roundtables: Regular local roundtables where employers, high schools, community colleges, universities, and training providers map current and emerging skill needs, co-design curricula, and commit to concrete co-op/apprenticeship slots. The community organizes and documents outcomes so training aligns to local demand.
Address: 134 Eileen Stubbs Avenue, Unit 103, Dartmouth, NS B3B 2C8

Program: Faculty of Computer Science External Advisory Council and Co-op Employer Roundtables
Organization: Dalhousie University, Faculty of Computer Science
Description: Dalhousie’s Faculty of Computer Science convenes an External Advisory Council and recurring employer roundtables that include tech companies, startup leaders, and public-sector employers to map evolving competencies in fields like AI, cybersecurity, and data science. Feedback directly shapes course content and new credentials while employers commit to specific co-op and internship placements through the faculty’s co-op office; meeting outcomes and curriculum changes are documented and reviewe...
Solution: Community Employer-Education Roundtables: Regular local roundtables where employers, high schools, community colleges, universities, and training providers map current and emerging skill needs, co-design curricula, and commit to concrete co-op/apprenticeship slots. The community organizes and documents outcomes so training aligns to local demand.

Organization: Saint Mary’s University (Continuing Education / Executive & Professional Development)
Description: Saint Mary’s University offers micro-credentials through Continuing Education and Executive & Professional Development that target in-demand skills in business analysis, digital marketing, data, and leadership. Programs are created with employer advisory input from the Halifax region, produce verifiable digital badges, and are designed to be stackable toward advanced certificates, helping local businesses hire for proven, job-ready competencies.
Solution: Local Industry Micro‑credential Program: A community-managed stackable micro‑credential initiative developed with local businesses to certify specific, job‑ready skills (short courses, badges) that employers recognize and prioritize for hiring and promotions.

Program: SMU Entrepreneurship Centre – Student Employment Program (RBC Talent Fund)
Description: The SMU Entrepreneurship Centre brokers short-term internships and co-op-style placements for students with startups and SMEs across Nova Scotia, providing hands-on coordination from employer matching to onboarding. Through the RBC Talent Fund and related supports, the Centre offsets wages/stipends for small employers and delivers training and mentorship to students—operating as a shared WIL hub that makes placements financially and operationally feasible for local businesses.
Solution: Shared Work‑Integrated Learning (WIL) Hub: A municipal or non-profit run hub that brokers co-op, internship and apprenticeship placements among small employers, provides placement coordination, onboarding support, and small-stipend funding to make placements viable for local businesses.

Description: Acadia’s Co-op Program brokers paid work terms with employers across Nova Scotia—including many small businesses—by recruiting candidates, facilitating interviews, and coordinating learning objectives and onboarding. The program advises employers on wage-subsidy options (e.g., CEI/SWPP) and provides ongoing support to ensure high-quality placements, operating as a centralized WIL conduit that aligns student skills with real workplace needs.
Solution: Shared Work‑Integrated Learning (WIL) Hub: A municipal or non-profit run hub that brokers co-op, internship and apprenticeship placements among small employers, provides placement coordination, onboarding support, and small-stipend funding to make placements viable for local businesses.

Program: Trade Qualifier and Prior Learning Assessment
Organization: Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency (Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration)
Description: The Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency assesses prior work experience and competencies through the Trade Qualifier route, scheduling assessment days and practical exams so experienced workers and newcomers can challenge certification. Recognized hours and successful assessments lead to provincial trade certification or direct entry into apprenticeship, credentials that employers across Nova Scotia accept.
Solution: Recognition of Prior Learning (RPL) Clinics: Community centers offering regular RPL workshops and assessment days to help young people and newcomers convert informal, volunteer, or on-the-job experience into recognized credentials that local employers accept.

Description: Discovery Centre’s mobile outreach team brings portable maker and digital media kits—such as robotics, circuits, 3D design, and coding activities—to libraries, schools, and community hubs throughout rural Nova Scotia. These short, facilitated sessions provide hands-on, near-to-home training that strengthens digital literacy and creative tech skills, helping youth explore pathways into technology and creative industries.
Solution: Mobile Training and Maker Labs: A traveling training unit or pop-up maker lab that brings hands-on, short-term training (e.g., welding, coding bootcamps, digital media) to rural communities, lowering barriers to accessing in-demand skills nearby.
Address: 1215 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Description: Discovery Centre runs supervised, hands-on after-school clubs that immerse youth in science, technology, engineering, arts, and math through coding, robotics, maker projects, and design challenges. Staff and volunteer mentors provide guidance and role modelling, offering a structured, skill-focused environment that supports families by engaging older children into the early evening.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: After-School Skills and Mentorship Programs: Community-run after-school programs that combine supervision with trades, arts or tech mentorship, keeping older children engaged while parents work or study.
Address: 1215 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Organization: Nova Scotia Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration
Description: The Co-operative Education Incentive provides wage subsidies to employers that hire co-op students from Nova Scotia post-secondary institutions. By cost-sharing student wages, the program effectively matches employer contributions to create paid placements, reducing the financial barrier for SMEs and nonprofits. This matching approach expands the number of quality co-op opportunities and aligns student skills with employer needs.
Solution: Employer-Funded Stipend Matching Pool: A community-managed fund that matches small employer contributions to provide stipends for co-op students and apprentices, making placements financially sustainable for businesses and accessible to youth.

Program: Nova Scotia Works – Opportunity Place Resource Association
Organization: Opportunity Place Resource Association (Nova Scotia Works)
Description: This Nova Scotia Works centre offers a one-stop hub in Dartmouth (with virtual access) where youth and jobseekers explore local career pathways, get personalized career counselling, and connect to employers posting real-time openings. Staff support applications to apprenticeships/co-ops, help clients access training and wage subsidies, and guide them to short courses and micro-credentials aligned with regional employer needs.
Solution: Local Career Navigation Centers: One-stop community centers (physical + virtual) that help youth explore local career pathways, apply for co-ops/apprenticeships, access training funds, and connect to employers with real-time openings and micro-credential options.
Address: 33 Ochterloney Street, Suite 210, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 4P5

Program: Nova Scotia Works Labour Market Information and Job Board
Organization: Nova Scotia Department of Labour, Skills and Immigration (Nova Scotia Works)
Description: Nova Scotia Works maintains a province-wide, publicly accessible job board and labour market information hub that aggregates real-time vacancies, highlights in-demand occupations, and surfaces the top skills employers are seeking across regions. The dashboard and reports are used by community partners and training providers to align programs with short- and long-term employer needs, helping students and job seekers choose pathways that match projected vacancies and priority skills.
Solution: Community Skills Forecast and Vacancy Board: A publicly accessible local dashboard maintained by community partners showing short-term and long-term employer needs, projected vacancies, and priority skills — used to guide training providers and student choices.

Description: Dalhousie University’s Management Without Borders is a for-credit, interdisciplinary project course where graduate students collaborate with external organizations to solve real management, policy, and community challenges. Client partners from business, government, and non-profits co-define deliverables, ensuring students apply classroom learning to practical needs that employers value.
Solution: School-Enterprise Project Partnerships: Programs where schools partner with local businesses and non-profits on real projects (product design, service delivery, community events) that count for credit and provide tangible experience employers value.

Description: NSCAD University’s design studio courses regularly engage students in client-based projects for local companies, social enterprises, and arts organizations, with outcomes such as visual identities, product concepts, and campaign assets. These engagements are structured for academic credit, aligning design curriculum with real market briefs and professional workflows.
Solution: School-Enterprise Project Partnerships: Programs where schools partner with local businesses and non-profits on real projects (product design, service delivery, community events) that count for credit and provide tangible experience employers value.

Description: NSCAD University places recent graduates and practicing artists as community artists-in-residence in towns across Nova Scotia, where they deliver workshops, class visits, and collaborative projects with local schools, libraries, and community centres. Residents receive studio space and paid opportunities to teach, mentor youth, and run public programs, directly generating income for artists while expanding arts access. The program strengthens local cultural ecosystems and connects young peopl...
Challenge: Support for Arts, Culture, and Creative Industries
Solution: Artist-Teacher and Artist-in-Residence Partnerships: Place practicing artists in schools, libraries, and community centers for residencies that offer paid teaching, public workshops, and collaborative community projects. This creates income for artists, arts exposure for youth, and stronger community ties to creative practice.

Description: Ready2Launch is Dal Innovates’ summer accelerator that pays student teams to work full-time on building their ventures while receiving mentorship, structured workshops, and access to university co-working and prototyping resources. The paid work-study model provides practical startup experience and industry-recognized work-integrated learning, directly addressing skills mismatches and easing school-to-work transitions.
Solution: Youth Entrepreneurship Incubator with Work-Study: A community incubator that supports young entrepreneurs with mentoring, space, and short-term paid work-study placements within startups, combining entrepreneurial skill-building with workplace experience recognized by local industry.

Program: SMU Entrepreneurship Centre – Work Integrated Learning (WIL) Programs
Description: The SMU Entrepreneurship Centre runs Work Integrated Learning programs that place students in paid, short-term roles with startups and small businesses while providing coaching, venture-building supports, and access to the Spark Zone sandbox community and space. By combining mentorship, entrepreneurial training, and real workplace experience inside local startups, the Centre helps students align skills with employer needs and explore launching ventures of their own.
Solution: Youth Entrepreneurship Incubator with Work-Study: A community incubator that supports young entrepreneurs with mentoring, space, and short-term paid work-study placements within startups, combining entrepreneurial skill-building with workplace experience recognized by local industry.

Description: HRM’s District 8 uses participatory budgeting to direct a share of district capital funds to projects chosen by residents, with outreach that encourages youth-led proposals and youth participation in voting. The process elevates local youth priorities—such as safe spaces, programming, culture, and recreation—through project pitches and public decision-making. By publishing results and funding decisions, it enhances transparency and keeps spending aligned with community needs identified by you...
Solution: Participatory Budgeting for Youth Priorities: Allocate a portion of municipal or community organization budgets for participatory budgeting processes focused on youth-led projects, increasing transparency, aligning spending with community needs, and fostering sustained civic engagement.

Program: Student Line of Credit and Personal Loans
Description: East Coast Credit Union is a member-owned financial cooperative that offers student lines of credit with interest-only payments while in school, plus low-rate personal loans and savings accounts designed to help members build small-scale savings and access emergency funds without resorting to high-interest credit. By operating as a cooperative, it returns value to members and partners in community finance initiatives, aligning with peer- and community-based finance models that reduce borrowin...
Solution: Peer Savings Groups and Cooperative Finance Models: Promote rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCA), cooperative banking products, and credit-union partnerships that enable small-scale savings and emergency lending without high interest.

Program: Student Line of Credit and Everyday Banking for Students
Description: Valley Credit Union offers cooperative banking services including a student line of credit, low-fee accounts, and small personal loans that enable members to save and borrow affordably during school and early career stages. Its member-owned model prioritizes financial well-being over profit, providing access to emergency credit and savings tools without the predatory rates often found in conventional short-term lending.
Solution: Peer Savings Groups and Cooperative Finance Models: Promote rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCA), cooperative banking products, and credit-union partnerships that enable small-scale savings and emergency lending without high interest.

Program: Small Business Advisory Services & Training (Digital and E‑commerce)
Organization: Centre for Women in Business (Mount Saint Vincent University)
Description: The Centre for Women in Business provides one-on-one advisory, peer cohorts, and hands-on workshops that help women-owned small businesses build or improve online storefronts, set up digital payment systems, and implement online booking and client management tools. Advisors work with retailers, trades and creatives across Nova Scotia—including rural communities—to choose platforms (e.g., Shopify, Squarespace, Square), integrate shipping and inventory, and develop digital marketing and remote-...
Solution: Local Business Digitalization and E‑commerce Clinics: Provide tailored support for local shops, trades and artists to establish online storefronts, digital payment systems and remote-client workflows so improved internet directly boosts local economic opportunities.

Program: Cape Breton – Unama’ki: Live, Work, Study
Description: The Cape Breton Partnership’s talent attraction initiative showcases the island’s lifestyle, Mi’kmaq culture, and real career opportunities through storytelling, videos, and community ambassador outreach. It pairs quality-of-life marketing with practical relocation supports (job board, welcoming network) to attract and retain young people and returning expats to make Cape Breton – Unama’ki their long-term home.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Place-Based Branding & Talent Campaigns: Develop community-led marketing that highlights local quality of life, career success stories and cultural strengths to reframe the region as an attractive long-term home for young people.

Description: Eastern Front Theatre’s Playwrights Unit brings together emerging playwrights with established dramaturgs and theatre professionals for regular feedback, script development, and portfolio reviews. Participants take part in professional workshops covering topics like grant writing, producing, and marketing, building a mentorship network that connects new voices with the practical skills and relationships needed for long-term careers.
Challenge: Support for Arts, Culture, and Creative Industries
Solution: Creative Skills and Mentorship Network: Build a volunteer-run network connecting established artists and tradespeople with emerging creatives for mentorship, portfolio reviews, and skills-sharing sessions (technical production, grant writing, marketing) to help young artists build sustainable careers.

Organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
Description: The Creative Entrepreneurship Program at Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design provides coaching, mentorship, and cohort-based training to help craft artists develop business plans, pricing, marketing, and export strategies. It also offers shared administrative services through its retail gallery and e-commerce channels—centralized point-of-sale, consignment management, and invoicing support—reducing overhead for emerging creative enterprises and enabling sustainable growth and employment.
Challenge: Support for Arts, Culture, and Creative Industries
Solution: Creative Enterprise Incubator: Launch a locally focused incubator offering business coaching, grant navigation, shared admin services (ticketing, booking, invoicing), and mentorship for arts entrepreneurs and creative startups to increase sustainability and job creation among young creators.

Organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
Description: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design’s Public Art Program commissions murals and installations throughout downtown Sydney in collaboration with business and property owners. The Centre manages artist selection, contracting, and project delivery, and works with local partners to provide funding and promotion—enabling businesses to host commissioned public art that enhances storefronts, increases foot traffic, and creates paid opportunities for artists.
Challenge: Support for Arts, Culture, and Creative Industries
Solution: Business-Artist Partnership Program: Facilitate partnerships between local businesses and artists for storefront activations, commissioned public art, in-store performances, and event sponsorships. Offer incentives to businesses (promotion, recognition, tax guidance) to lower barriers to collaboration.

Organization: Cape Breton Centre for Craft & Design
Description: Working with property owners and the downtown business district, this program curates rotating artisan and craft pop-ups in temporarily vacant storefronts along Charlotte Street, especially during evenings and weekends. These short-term shops and exhibitions activate idle retail spaces, provide low-cost opportunities for local creatives, and attract residents back to the core with music, markets, and cultural programming.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Pop-up events in vacant storefronts: Organize rotating weekend or evening pop-ups (food, craft markets, music, exhibitions) in empty retail spaces. Run by community groups and local entrepreneurs, these activate downtowns, support small vendors, and create low-cost nightlife without long-term commercial leases.

Program: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts – Artist Residencies & Creative Campus
Organization: Ross Creek Centre for the Arts
Description: Ross Creek provides multidisciplinary artist residencies with studio space, accommodations, and community-engaged projects on a rural arts campus. Year-round workshops, exhibitions, and partnerships with Two Planks and a Passion Theatre bring visitors to Kings County while creating ongoing creative and technical jobs. The cluster model links studios, residencies, public programming, and seasonal productions to sustain arts livelihoods beyond urban centres.
Solution: Arts and culture clusters with residencies: Support creative industries through shared studio space, artist residencies, public art commissions and coordinated events that create year-round creative jobs and attract visitors.
Address: 555 Ross Creek Road, Canning, NS B0P 1H0

Program: Summer Student Employment (Museum Interpreters and Program Assistants)
Organization: Black Cultural Centre for Nova Scotia
Description: The Black Cultural Centre hires local youth as paid museum interpreters, archives assistants, and event/program staff to support exhibits, tours, and cultural programming that preserve and share African Nova Scotian heritage. These roles provide professional experience in the cultural sector, strengthen community connection and pride, and illustrate sustainable careers in arts, heritage, and community service within Nova Scotia.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Civic Learning & Community Service Pathways: Create paid youth positions in municipal projects, cultural organizations and non-profits to build local leadership, deepen civic ties, and demonstrate viable careers that contribute to community life.
Address: 10 Cherry Brook Road, Cherry Brook, NS B2Z 1A8

Description: The Youth Project provides employer training to build 2SLGBTQIA+ inclusive recruitment, policies, and day-to-day practices. Sessions are co-led by queer and trans facilitators with lived experience, include reviews of job ads and onboarding materials for bias, and offer guidance on accommodations (e.g., affirmed names/pronouns, gender-affirming care) and retention strategies that create culturally safe workplaces.
Solution: Employer Training: Inclusive Recruitment and Retention: Organize peer-led workshops for local employers covering anti‑bias recruitment, accommodations, culturally safe workplaces, flexible scheduling and retention strategies, with community members as co-trainers and auditors.

Description: Ulnooweg supports Mi’kmaq and other Indigenous entrepreneurs with tailored financing, business advisory, mentorship, and capacity-building, including guidance to access procurement opportunities and partnerships. By combining culturally grounded advisory with flexible capital and ecosystem navigation, the program advances Indigenous-owned start-ups and small businesses across Nova Scotia.
Solution: Microgrants and Start‑Up Support for Underrepresented Entrepreneurs: Provide small grants, business mentoring, shared workspaces and procurement supports targeting Black, Indigenous, newcomer, 2SLGBTQIA+ and disabled entrepreneurs to grow local businesses and jobs.

Description: The North Grove’s family support workers assist Dartmouth North residents in accessing healthcare and mental health services by booking appointments, explaining referrals, and helping complete intake and benefits forms. Staff and volunteers also connect people to public health nurses, primary care, community programs, and transportation options (e.g., transit planning and access to local resources) to reduce barriers to care.
Solution: Community health navigator program: Local volunteers and social-service workers help residents—especially youth and newcomers—book appointments, understand referrals, complete intake forms, and connect to community resources and transportation options.

Program: Community Food Centre Market and Pantry
Description: The North Grove runs community food access programs that include an affordable market and a pantry-style distribution of donated and rescued foods like produce and bread. Working with local grocers, farms, and provincial food recovery partners, they redistribute surplus foods to Dartmouth North residents. These programs help reduce grocery bills for families and young people while cutting down on food waste.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Fridges and Food Rescue Partnerships: Neighbourhood fridges, pantry nodes and partnerships with grocery stores, restaurants and campuses to redistribute surplus food to residents, reducing household grocery expense and waste.

Program: Clean Energy Financing (PACE) – Nova Scotia Municipalities
Description: Clean Foundation partners with Nova Scotia municipalities to offer Property Assessed Clean Energy (PACE) financing that enables homeowners to undertake energy retrofits—such as heat pumps, insulation, windows/doors, and controls—with approved contractors. By spreading costs on the property tax bill and coordinating projects across communities, the program accelerates bulk retrofits that lower electricity demand and peak loads, easing grid constraints while improving home comfort.
Challenge: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth
Solution: Community Energy Efficiency Retrofits: Coordinate bulk retrofit programs (insulation, heat pumps, LED lighting, smart thermostats) for homes, schools and small businesses to cut electricity demand and reduce the need for new grid capacity.

Description: ACAP Cape Breton annually hires local youth for paid seasonal roles that deliver hands-on community environmental projects—such as shoreline cleanups, urban greening, trail and stream restoration, and public outreach—often in partnership with the Cape Breton Regional Municipality and neighbourhood organizations. The program builds leadership and work experience rooted in place while demonstrating how environmental stewardship can be a meaningful, locally based career path.
Challenge: Brain Drain to Larger Markets and Remote Employers
Solution: Civic Learning & Community Service Pathways: Create paid youth positions in municipal projects, cultural organizations and non-profits to build local leadership, deepen civic ties, and demonstrate viable careers that contribute to community life.

Program: ACAP Cape Breton – Community Advisory and Coordination Tables
Description: ACAP Cape Breton acts as a coordinating hub that brings together Cape Breton Regional Municipality departments, Indigenous communities, local businesses, post-secondary institutions, and youth and community groups to plan and deliver environmental and community development projects. Through recurring advisory committees and cross-sector roundtables, ACAP aligns priorities (e.g., coastal resilience, green jobs, neighborhood revitalization) and coordinates implementation, ensuring initiatives m...
Solution: Local Cross-Sector Coordination Councils: Form neighbourhood or regional councils made up of municipal staff, community organizations, business leaders, post-secondary representatives, Indigenous partners, and youth to meet regularly, align priorities, and coordinate local initiatives so projects move from idea to implementation faster and with shared accountability.

Program: Clean Foundation – Energy Advisor and Clean Energy Training
Description: Clean Foundation delivers employer-aligned short courses that prepare participants for green jobs, including training pathways toward NRCan Home Energy Advisor credentials and practical upskilling in efficiency and heat pump fundamentals. Offered online and in communities across Nova Scotia in partnership with organizations like Efficiency Nova Scotia and local employers, the training provides stackable, industry-recognized credentials that connect learners to real hiring needs.
Solution: Micro-credential and Short-course Consortium: A partnership of community colleges, training centres and employers offering stackable, industry-vetted micro-credentials for tech, trades, care and green jobs that can be earned locally or online.

Description: Through programs like HomeWarming, Clean Foundation trains partner organizations’ outreach staff and community ambassadors to gather standardized household data on energy efficiency, housing conditions, and energy affordability across Nova Scotia. Clean curates and analyzes these data to produce community-level insights that are shared with municipalities and the Province, informing housing, climate, and affordability policy while closing data gaps for underserved communities.
Solution: Community Data Stewards Program: Train volunteers and staff from local organizations to collect, curate, and interpret community-level data (surveys, vacancy rates, youth employment outcomes) so data gaps shrink and local evidence feeds into higher-level policy conversations.

Description: Nova Scotia Power offers an education assistance benefit that reimburses tuition and related costs for approved certificates, diplomas, and degree programs, and supports apprentices with time for in‑class training. These employer-provided education supports and flexible work options allow early‑career employees to upskill while earning, reducing debt pressures and helping retain talent in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Local Employer Tuition Reimbursement and Flexible Hiring: Encourage area employers to offer tuition reimbursement, continuing education stipends, and flexible schedules for early-career workers, reducing pressure to leave for higher pay elsewhere.
Address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Description: Nova Scotia Power’s Joint Use program enables wireless providers and community partners to attach small-cell radios, repeaters, and related equipment to utility poles and other NSP assets across the province. The program manages engineering standards, safety, and permitting, providing a practical pathway for community-level deployments that enhance cellular coverage in rural and hard-to-serve areas.
Solution: Community Cell Boosters and Small‑Cell Deployments: Identify strategic community-owned locations (halls, water towers, municipal buildings) where small cellular nodes or signal boosters can be installed to improve mobile coverage. Organize permits, site stewardship and cost-sharing among users.
Address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Program: Net Metering Interconnection – Pre‑Certified Equipment and Standard Packages
Description: Nova Scotia Power’s net metering program maintains standardized interconnection requirements and accepts pre‑certified inverters and equipment, enabling installers to use repeatable, utility‑approved solar PV packages with standard single‑line diagrams. This acts as a pre‑approved design library for small renewable systems, cutting review time and simplifying municipal and utility approvals for common rooftop installations.
Solution: Pre‑Approved Local Design Library: Develop a set of common, pre‑approved designs for tiny homes, accessory units, renewable installations and small commercial fitouts that municipalities can endorse to speed approvals for repeatable projects.
Address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Program: Nova Scotia Power Interruptible Load Rider
Description: For large commercial and industrial customers, Nova Scotia Power provides an interruptible/curtailable service option that offers bill credits in exchange for reducing load when the utility calls peak events. Facilities use building automation, process scheduling, or thermal storage to temporarily curtail demand during the highest-stress hours, responding to clear price signals and event notices. This demand-response program directly lowers peak demand on the provincial grid and complements b...
Challenge: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth
Solution: Local Demand‑Response and Time‑of‑Use Programs: Organize community campaigns and incentives to shift discretionary electricity use (water heating, EV charging, appliances) to off‑peak hours using smart timers and price signals, lowering peak stress on the grid.
Address: 1223 Lower Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 3S8

Description: Nova Scotia Power’s interconnection services team runs ongoing stakeholder engagements and technical consultations with municipalities, renewable developers, and customers to identify bottlenecks in connecting distributed and community-scale projects. Through updated standards, pre-application reviews, and streamlined workflows for small generators and net-metered systems, the utility co-designs and pilots faster approval processes that reduce interconnection timelines and clarify requirement...
Challenge: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth
Solution: Interconnection Working Group (Community + Utility): Create a local forum of municipalities, developers, utilities and residents to map interconnection pain points, co‑design streamlined processes, and pilot faster approval workflows for small and community projects.

Program: Stormwater and Coastal Flood Resilience Initiatives (including Adopt-A-Drain Lunenburg County)
Description: Coastal Action mobilizes volunteers to survey and map flooding hotspots across Lunenburg County—documenting flooded basements, blocked culverts, vulnerable streets, and critical access routes—through initiatives like Adopt‑A‑Drain and community flood‑watch activities. The organization compiles these observations into GIS layers and public story maps, and delivers workshops, flyers, and business/homeowner toolkits that explain localized flood risks, detour routes, and practical property-level ...
Solution: Community flood mapping and risk communication: Volunteer-driven mapping of high-risk streets, basements and access routes combined with clear, locally distributed guidance so residents, prospective homebuyers and insurers understand true risk and adaptation options.

Description: Coastal Action works with homeowners and communities on the South Shore to reduce overland flooding through site assessments, rain gardens, downspout reconfiguration, grading, and other lot-level measures. They coordinate volunteer work bees and bulk purchasing of materials and native plants, lowering costs for residents undertaking flood-proofing retrofits. Staff provide technical advice that helps households plan and implement practical measures like sump pump maintenance, backflow preventi...
Solution: Home retrofit and elevation co-op: A community co-op that helps pool labour, tool lending, group purchasing and technical advice for flood-proofing, elevating homes and installing sump pumps to lower repair costs and insurance claims.

Description: Coastal Action trains residents, students, and staff from partner community organizations to collect long-term water quality and habitat data throughout the LaHave River watershed and nearby communities. The organization curates and analyzes the data, shares results with municipalities and provincial regulators, and uses the evidence to guide management actions and policy advocacy—building local data stewardship capacity and feeding community evidence into policy conversations.
Solution: Community Data Stewards Program: Train volunteers and staff from local organizations to collect, curate, and interpret community-level data (surveys, vacancy rates, youth employment outcomes) so data gaps shrink and local evidence feeds into higher-level policy conversations.

Organization: Dalhousie University, Department of Family Medicine
Description: Dalhousie Medicine’s Rural Week places first-year medical students with preceptors in rural Nova Scotia communities for immersive, work-integrated learning. Local host families and community partners commonly provide billeted or no-cost housing and community-based supports, reducing accommodation costs so students can complete rural placements and explore careers in underserved areas.
Solution: Rural Placement Incentives and Housing Supports: Locally funded stipends, short-term housing or host-family programs to remove cost and accommodation barriers for rural placements and internships.

Program: Killam Apartment REIT Resident EV Charging
Description: Killam Apartment REIT is deploying shared EV charging hubs at multi-unit residential buildings in Halifax and across Nova Scotia. The installations use smart, networked chargers with dynamic load balancing to keep total current within each building’s electrical capacity and to avoid costly service upgrades; residents use an app to manage access and queueing, ensuring fair use of limited ports. Challenge: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth

Description: The Town of Kentville runs a recurring summer Night Market series that animates Centre Square and nearby closed streets with Nova Scotian artisans, food trucks, and live music. By activating public space in the evening with affordable vendor fees and performance slots, the market creates low-barrier, pop-up earning opportunities for local makers and musicians while helping them build audiences.
Challenge: Support for Arts, Culture, and Creative Industries
Solution: Pop-Up Festivals and Night Markets: Organize regular, low-cost pop-up festivals and night markets that prioritize local musicians, makers, and food vendors. Use public parks, waterfronts, and closed streets to create recurring opportunities for creatives to earn income and build audiences.

Program: NSFM Regional Caucus Meetings and Annual Conference
Description: The Nova Scotia Federation of Municipalities convenes regular regional caucus meetings (rural, towns, and regional municipalities) and an annual conference that bring together municipal staff, elected officials, and provincial department representatives to exchange lessons and align on priority files. These forums surface common challenges, harmonize approaches across jurisdictions, and generate shared toolkits and templates (e.g., on housing, asset management, and climate adaptation) that re...
Solution: Regular Knowledge-Sharing Forums: Host quarterly forums where municipal staff, community groups, and provincial representatives exchange lessons, harmonize approaches, and create shared toolkits — reducing siloed practice and speeding adoption of proven policies.
Address: 1809 Barrington Street, Suite 1106, Halifax, NS B3J 3K8

Program: Municipal Planning Services and Bylaw Updates
Description: EDPC provides planning services to several Nova Scotia municipalities, leading community consultations and drafting Municipal Planning Strategies and Land‑Use Bylaws that can incorporate density bonusing for affordable units and reduced parking requirements in town centres. By aligning zoning with transit and services, EDPC helps councils adopt reforms that enable more diverse, attainable housing in the right places.
Solution: Inclusionary Zoning and Planning Advocacy: Organize community campaigns to work with municipalities to adopt inclusionary zoning, density bonuses and reduced parking rules to increase the supply of affordable units near services and transit.
Address: 606 Reeves Street, Unit 3, Port Hawkesbury, NS B9A 2R7

Description: The Loaded Ladle serves free or pay-what-you-can vegan lunches for students and community members from a shared campus kitchen at Dalhousie University. Volunteer-led prep shifts teach cooking and organizing skills, while bulk purchasing and donated produce lower costs and help prevent food waste.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Kitchens and Shared Meal Programs: Shared commercial kitchen hours, meal prep co-ops, and pay-what-you-can community dinners run by local organizations to lower meal costs, build skills, and reduce food waste.

Description: The Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency provides living, travel, and accommodation allowances to apprentices who must train away from home, including those from rural communities attending technical training or work placements. These stipends reduce out-of-pocket costs for temporary housing and travel, enabling rural apprentices in trades to complete required training aligned with employer demand.
Solution: Rural Placement Incentives and Housing Supports: Locally funded stipends, short-term housing or host-family programs to remove cost and accommodation barriers for rural placements and internships.

Description: Mentorship Matters equips experienced journeypersons—often late-career or semi-retired—with practical tools to mentor apprentices on the job. Employers use the training to formalize reduced-hours mentoring roles for senior tradespeople, supporting phased retirement while transferring critical tacit skills in construction and skilled trades. The program strengthens succession planning and shortens ramp-up time for new workers, directly addressing labour shortages.
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: Phased Retirement and Knowledge-Transfer Program: Enable phased retirement arrangements where senior workers retain part-time mentoring roles while training successors, ensuring institutional knowledge stays local.

Program: Community Garden, Greenhouse & Bulk Food Program
Description: The New Ross Family Resource Centre maintains on-site community gardens and a teaching greenhouse where residents grow and share produce while learning food skills. They partner with local farms to source seasonal surplus for low- or no-cost community meals and a bulk-buy food program, distributing fresh produce through a trusted community hub to help reduce household food expenses.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Gardens, Gleaning Networks and Farm Partnerships: Neighbourhood gardens on municipal or church land, paired with gleaning programs that collect surplus from local farms and distribute it through community hubs, increasing access to fresh produce and reducing grocery bills.

Description: A Nova Scotia Works employment centre that publishes a continuously updated local ‘Hot Jobs’ listing with wage or salary details, hours, contract length, and benefits when provided by employers. Staff collaborate with local businesses to include transparent job quality metrics and tag roles by full-time/part-time/seasonal status, helping jobseekers compare opportunities and recognize employers offering better terms.
Challenge: Wage Growth and Job Quality Gap
Solution: Local Wage Transparency Portal: Build a community-run online portal that lists local job quality metrics (wages, hours, benefits, advancement opportunities) to empower jobseekers, encourage competition on quality, and spotlight employers improving terms.
Address: 7051 Bayers Road, Suite 501, Halifax, NS B3L 4V2

Description: Easter Seals Nova Scotia operates accessible, door-to-door transportation for medical, therapy, and mental-health appointments, using lift-equipped vehicles and trained drivers. By providing reliable rides for people with mobility or other disabilities, the service removes a key barrier to accessing timely primary and mental-health care.
Solution: Volunteer transportation and ride-share for appointments: Volunteer driver programs and organized ride-share networks help people get to primary care and mental-health appointments, reducing missed visits and waitlist delays due to transportation barriers.

Program: Ulnooweg Education Centre – Indigenous STEAM & Entrepreneurship Programs
Description: Ulnooweg Education Centre co-designs STEAM and entrepreneurship training with Mi’kmaw communities across Nova Scotia, integrating Two-Eyed Seeing (Etuaptmumk), language, and land-based learning into hands-on programs. Youth and young adults build skills in coding, robotics, environmental monitoring, and business while working with Elders, Knowledge Keepers, and local mentors. The programs create clear pathways to further education, internships, and jobs with community organizations and region...
Solution: Indigenous-led and Culturally Relevant Training Programs: Locally designed programs co-created with Indigenous communities that integrate cultural knowledge, language and priorities into training and pathways.

Description: Digital Mi'kmaq partners with Mi'kmaw communities to deliver supervised, culturally grounded after-school STEM clubs that introduce coding, engineering, digital fabrication, and data literacy. Experienced mentors and educators provide hands-on learning and career exposure in technology fields, supporting families by engaging Indigenous youth in constructive after-school programming.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: After-School Skills and Mentorship Programs: Community-run after-school programs that combine supervision with trades, arts or tech mentorship, keeping older children engaged while parents work or study.

Description: The Town of Kentville’s citizen-led Diversity Advisory Committee includes residents and stakeholder representatives from equity-deserving communities who advise Council on anti-racism, equity, accessibility, and inclusion. The committee reviews municipal policies and services for systemic barriers, proposes policy and bylaw changes, supports community education and training on inclusion, and monitors progress on the Town’s inclusion goals through reports and recommendations.
Solution: Community Anti-Racism & Inclusion Task Force: Create a citizen-led task force made up of representatives from Black, Mi’kmaq, newcomer, 2SLGBTQIA+, disability and youth communities to audit local institutions, propose policy changes, coordinate community education, and monitor progress on inclusion goals.

Program: Food Truck Friday at the Barn (Hubbards)
Description: The Hubbards Barn Association runs weekly evening Food Truck Fridays with multiple local vendors, live music, and family-friendly space on the Barn grounds. These extended-hours nights draw residents and visitors for a casual community ‘night out,’ supporting local food entrepreneurs and creating regular, safe nighttime activity in a shared public venue.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Evening markets and extended-hours nights: Coordinate monthly evening markets, themed 'night out' events or late-shopping nights with local businesses, street performances, and family-friendly activities to create regular safe nightlife options.

Program: Coastal Land Acquisition and Protection Program
Description: The Nova Scotia Nature Trust acquires vulnerable coastal properties from willing sellers and places them under permanent protection, preventing redevelopment in high-risk locations. These voluntary purchases convert shorelines into conserved natural buffers that absorb storm impacts and sea-level rise while providing public ecological benefits—an on-the-ground, managed-retreat approach that reduces future property loss and insurance risk.
Solution: Planned buyouts and voluntary managed retreat program: A locally managed, transparent program offering fair purchase or relocation support for repeatedly damaged properties, converting vulnerable land to public green space or coastal buffers.
Address: 81 Prince Albert Road, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1M1

Description: The Unama’ki Institute of Natural Resources (UINR) delivers Indigenous-led training for Guardians, fisheries and forestry technicians, and environmental monitors grounded in Mi’kmaw knowledge and language. Programs emphasize Netukulimk principles and land-based learning while providing certifications and work placements tied to regional employers in conservation, fisheries, and protected areas. This creates culturally relevant pathways from community learning to stable jobs in green and resou...
Solution: Indigenous-led and Culturally Relevant Training Programs: Locally designed programs co-created with Indigenous communities that integrate cultural knowledge, language and priorities into training and pathways.

Program: Food Bank and Mobile Food Bank
Description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank distributes weekly food hampers with pantry staples and fresh items, combining bulk-purchased and donated foods to reduce costs for clients. Its Mobile Food Bank extends low-cost and no-cost distribution into multiple neighborhoods, improving access for youth and families affected by rising living expenses. The program’s centralized procurement and regular distribution align with a bulk-buy model that keeps staple foods affordable.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Food Co-op and Bulk-Buy Program: A member-run grocery co-op that aggregates bulk purchases from regional suppliers (including Maritime producers) to lower grocery costs, offers sliding-scale memberships for youth, and hosts weekly low-cost pantry staples distribution.

Description: Parker Street Food & Furniture Bank runs a free income tax preparation program for low-income individuals and families, ensuring clients file accurately and access refundable credits and benefits. The organization also provides drop-in support to review bills and budgets and connects people with subsidies and partner agencies for debt counselling to help stabilize household finances.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Financial Literacy, Benefits Navigation and Tax Clinics: Regular community workshops and drop-in clinics that teach budgeting, debt management, claims for provincial/federal benefits, and how to access eligible subsidies to improve net income.

Program: Yarmouth Hospital Foundation Health Professional Bursary Program
Description: Funded by community donations and local business support, this program offers bursaries to students training for high‑need health roles with a commitment to work in the Tri‑County area after graduation. Recipients sign return‑of‑service agreements tied to positions at Yarmouth Regional Hospital or partner care sites, channeling local philanthropy into stable, community‑based health careers.
Solution: Community-funded Scholarships and Bursaries: Create locally governed scholarship and bursary pools (donor circles, employer contributions, municipal seed funds) targeted at students who commit to living or working in the community for a set period after graduation.

Description: The Foundation mobilizes community crowdfunding—small gifts from residents and contributions from local businesses—often boosted by matching challenges during peak campaigns, to fund bursaries for students pursuing health careers. Awards help cover tuition and related costs so recipients can avoid or reduce student debt, with a focus on learners who commit to return to work in the Antigonish area’s health system.
Solution: Crowdfunding Platforms and Matching Days for Debt Relief: Coordinate local crowdfunding campaigns and matching-fund events where businesses and residents contribute to clearing critical student debts for individuals who promise to stay and work locally.

Description: The Town of Yarmouth’s Diversity and Inclusion Committee engages residents and stakeholder representatives, including voices from African Nova Scotian, Mi’kmaw, newcomer, 2SLGBTQIA+, disability, and youth communities, to advance a more inclusive municipality. The committee reviews Town policies and programs to identify barriers, recommends changes and best practices, helps coordinate public education and cultural awareness activities, and reports to Council on progress toward inclusion goals.
Solution: Community Anti-Racism & Inclusion Task Force: Create a citizen-led task force made up of representatives from Black, Mi’kmaq, newcomer, 2SLGBTQIA+, disability and youth communities to audit local institutions, propose policy changes, coordinate community education, and monitor progress on inclusion goals.

Program: Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB) – Atlantic Canada Office
Description: CFIB mobilizes thousands of Nova Scotia small businesses to advocate for provincial policies that reduce payroll costs and strengthen job quality, including tax reforms, training incentives, and targeted wage supports. Members receive direct access to business advisors for HR compliance guidance, compensation and benefits planning, and navigation of provincial and federal programs—practical coaching that helps small employers sustainably increase wages and expand benefits.
Challenge: Wage Growth and Job Quality Gap
Solution: Local Policy Advocacy & Small Business Supports: Mobilize community coalitions to advocate for provincial supports (tax credits, wage subsidies) that help small employers improve pay and benefits, while offering local HR and financial coaching to make implementation feasible.

Description: A mobile library service that parks at scheduled stops throughout Cumberland County to deliver free Wi‑Fi access alongside borrowing services. The team helps patrons with digital tasks—such as accessing online classes, setting up devices, and navigating government services—while lending materials and, where available, take-home hotspots or devices.
Solution: Mobile Wi‑Fi Outreach (School Buses, Libraries-on-Wheels): Deploy Wi‑Fi-equipped vehicles or library-bus services that park at neighbourhood hub points on scheduled days to provide internet access, device lending and digital help for remote learners and residents without home service.

Description: reachAbility trains employers to recruit and retain persons with disabilities through anti-bias hiring practices, duty-to-accommodate guidance, accessible job design, and flexible scheduling strategies. Workshops are peer-led by facilitators with disabilities and can include workplace accessibility audits and reviews of recruitment and onboarding materials to reduce barriers and improve retention.
Solution: Employer Training: Inclusive Recruitment and Retention: Organize peer-led workshops for local employers covering anti‑bias recruitment, accommodations, culturally safe workplaces, flexible scheduling and retention strategies, with community members as co-trainers and auditors.

These parent-participation programs cultivate reciprocal support networks where families share responsibilities and exchange care, creating reliable, community-based childcare that reduces stress and supports consistent work or study schedules.
Solution: Community childcare co-ops to reduce caregiver burnout: Neighbourhood-run childcare co-ops and reciprocal care networks give parents and young workers reliable, affordable childcare so they can attend appointments, rest, or maintain stable work schedules.

Program: Student Line of Credit and Youth Accounts
Description: Sydney Credit Union provides a Student Line of Credit with competitive rates and interest-only payments while in school, helping students and young workers finance tuition, tools, and training with lower monthly costs. Solution: Community Credit Union Programs and Matched-Savings: Partnerships with local credit unions to offer no-fee accounts, low-interest small loans, matched-savings programs for training or emergencies, and youth-friendly financial products.

Description: The Confederacy of Mainland Mi’kmaq’s Netukulimk Department designs and delivers training for Indigenous Guardians, climate action, fisheries, and environmental technician roles in mainland Mi’kmaw communities. Solution: Indigenous-led and Culturally Relevant Training Programs: Locally designed programs co-created with Indigenous communities that integrate cultural knowledge, language and priorities into training and pathways.

Description: Hike Nova Scotia coordinates year-round series of free and low-cost group hikes, walks, and snowshoe outings across the province, often in partnership with local clubs and parks. Many events emphasize mindfulness and nature-connection (including occasional forest bathing-style walks), helping participants lower stress, build social ties, and adopt healthy routines that complement clinical mental health care.
Solution: Arts- and nature-based therapeutic programs: Local arts organizations and parks groups offer group music, art, and outdoor programs (guided hikes, gardening, forest bathing) that lower stress, build social connection, and complement clinical care.

Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
