Many awards prioritize candidates who commit to practice in Colchester and East Hants after graduation, tying financial relief to a return‑of‑service that keeps talent working locally.
Solution: Crowdfunding Platforms and Matching Days for Debt Relief: Coordinate local crowdfunding campaigns and matching-fund events where businesses and residents contribute to clearing critical student debts for individuals who promise to stay and work locally.

Description: Backed by community crowdfunding events like the Because You Care Radiothon and Giving Tuesday–style match campaigns, the Foundation raises donor funds that are granted to Cape Breton students in health disciplines. These awards reduce tuition pressure and help recipients pay down student loans while encouraging or requiring return‑of‑service placements in Cape Breton’s hospitals and clinics, directly linking debt relief to staying and working locally.
Solution: Crowdfunding Platforms and Matching Days for Debt Relief: Coordinate local crowdfunding campaigns and matching-fund events where businesses and residents contribute to clearing critical student debts for individuals who promise to stay and work locally.

Description: Cape Breton Credit Union provides cooperative banking products such as a StudentLine of credit and small personal loans that offer fair, transparent rates and flexible repayment, helping members handle education costs and unexpected expenses. As a community-owned credit union, it emphasizes financial inclusion and savings-building tools, providing an alternative to high-cost payday and installment lenders for students and young workers.
Solution: Peer Savings Groups and Cooperative Finance Models: Promote rotating savings and credit associations (ROSCA), cooperative banking products, and credit-union partnerships that enable small-scale savings and emergency lending without high interest.

Organization: South End Day Care Co-operative Limited
Description: A parent-member co-operative that provides licensed early learning and child care where families share governance and help shape policies, schedules, and programming. By pooling member dues and participating in decision-making, the co-op keeps fees lower and can add flexible options like extended hours to meet local demand.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Community Childcare Cooperatives: Parents and neighbours form member-run cooperatives that share governance, staffing and costs to offer affordable, flexible care (including evenings) tailored to local demand.

Program: New Ross Family Resource Centre – Co-operative Preschool Program
Description: The centre facilitates a parent-participation preschool where caregivers share classroom duties and planning, and help guide policies through a member structure. By distributing responsibilities and costs among families, the program offers an affordable, community-tailored option that can adjust hours and supports based on local demand.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Community Childcare Cooperatives: Parents and neighbours form member-run cooperatives that share governance, staffing and costs to offer affordable, flexible care (including evenings) tailored to local demand.

Program: Dalhousie University Child Care Centre Society
Organization: Dalhousie University Child Care Centre Society
Description: A licensed, on-campus child care program that provides early learning spaces primarily for Dalhousie University employees and students. Operated in partnership with the university (which provides facilities and supports), the centres give staff priority access to nearby child care and schedules that align with work and academic calendars—an employer-supported model that reduces wait times and commuting barriers for working parents.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Employer-Supported Childcare Partnerships: Local employers partner with community groups to provide on-site or nearby childcare spaces, schedule flexibility, subsidies or employer-paid slots for staff.

Description: A campus-based, licensed childcare program that serves Acadia University employees and students with proximity-based access and enrollment priority. Supported through the university’s provision of space and collaboration on operations, the centre exemplifies an employer-enabled childcare option that shortens commutes, coordinates with work/study schedules, and improves workforce participation for parents.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Employer-Supported Childcare Partnerships: Local employers partner with community groups to provide on-site or nearby childcare spaces, schedule flexibility, subsidies or employer-paid slots for staff.

Program: Extended Hours Club Programs and School-Age Care
Organization: BGC Halifax (Boys & Girls Clubs of Greater Halifax)
Description: BGC Halifax operates licensed school-age child care alongside evening and occasional weekend club programs at its North End community hub. By keeping the centre open into the evening and offering supervised, program-based care staffed by trained youth workers and early childhood educators, the site gives parents working nonstandard shifts a safe, community-based option beyond typical daycare hours.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Extended-Hours Community Childcare Hubs: Libraries, recreation centres or community centres open licensed after-hours/weekend childcare programs staffed by trained local workers to cover nonstandard shifts.

Program: After-School and Evening Club Programs at East Dartmouth Community Centre
Description: BGC East Dartmouth operates out of the East Dartmouth Community Centre, providing licensed school-age care after school and extending access to supervised evening and Saturday programming. The community-centre setting and trained staff create a flexible, safe environment that supports parents who work irregular hours by offering care and engagement for children beyond the standard workday.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Extended-Hours Community Childcare Hubs: Libraries, recreation centres or community centres open licensed after-hours/weekend childcare programs staffed by trained local workers to cover nonstandard shifts.

Program: Dalhousie University MyCareer Job Board (Childcare & Casual Roles)
Organization: Dalhousie University – Student Career & Leadership Development
Description: Dalhousie’s MyCareer platform allows community members to post casual/part-time childcare roles that student caregivers can pick up in shared shifts. Parents can arrange nanny-shares or micro-pods by scheduling multiple students across the week and using transparent postings to outline hours and rates; payments are handled directly between families and caregivers.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Shared Caregiver Pooling Platform: A community app or bulletin board that helps parents coordinate shifts, share caregivers or form micro-pods with transparent scheduling and micro-payments.

Program: Saint Mary’s University Career & Experiential Learning – Career360 Job Board
Organization: Saint Mary’s University – Career & Experiential Learning
Description: SMU’s Career360 job board is open to local households posting babysitting and nanny-share opportunities that students can take on in coordinated shifts. The listing format supports clear schedules and rates, helping parents form small caregiver pods or share a sitter while arranging bookings and micro-payments directly with students.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Shared Caregiver Pooling Platform: A community app or bulletin board that helps parents coordinate shifts, share caregivers or form micro-pods with transparent scheduling and micro-payments.

Description: Cole Harbour Place coordinates daily bus/van pick-ups from area elementary schools and shuttles children directly to its After School Program. By providing supervised school-to-program transportation, it enables families living beyond walking distance to secure after-school childcare without needing a personal vehicle or mid-day work interruptions.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Community Transportation for Childcare Access: Organize shuttle services, carpool networks or voucher programs to help families get children to and from childcare sites outside walking distance.
Address: 51 Forest Hills Parkway, Dartmouth, NS B2W 6C6

Description: Zatzman Sportsplex offers an after-school program that includes organized pick-up from partner schools, transporting children by Sportsplex-operated buses/vans to the facility for care and activities. This shuttle service expands access for families who are not within walking distance or cannot leave work to drive.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Community Transportation for Childcare Access: Organize shuttle services, carpool networks or voucher programs to help families get children to and from childcare sites outside walking distance.

Description: The Rath Eastlink Community Centre runs an after-school program with daily transportation from local schools to the RECC via staff-driven buses/vans. This school-to-childcare shuttle removes a key barrier for working parents and supports consistent access to care for families living beyond walking distance.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Community Transportation for Childcare Access: Organize shuttle services, carpool networks or voucher programs to help families get children to and from childcare sites outside walking distance.

Description: New Dawn’s immigration team supports newcomer families with one-on-one settlement navigation, including finding licensed childcare, after-school programs, and culturally appropriate family resources in Cape Breton. They provide language access, family programming, and coordinated referrals to employment and training supports, helping parents enter or re-enter the workforce.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Newcomer-Focused Family Support Centres: Multilingual, culturally responsive hubs that provide childcare navigation, culturally appropriate programming and connections to settlement services and employment supports.

Program: Newcomer Services at Keshen Goodman Public Library
Description: Keshen Goodman Library hosts newcomer-focused family programs and multilingual supports, including information sessions on childcare options, school registration, and benefits, often delivered in partnership with settlement agencies. Librarians provide culturally responsive referrals to childcare and employment services and offer family-friendly spaces and activities that help parents balance learning, job search, and caregiving.
Challenge: Access to Childcare and Family Supports
Solution: Newcomer-Focused Family Support Centres: Multilingual, culturally responsive hubs that provide childcare navigation, culturally appropriate programming and connections to settlement services and employment supports.

Description: HOPES runs regular pop-up, no-cost primary care clinics hosted at a community health centre, staffed by supervised student volunteers and volunteer clinicians from multiple disciplines. The clinic offers basic primary care, vaccinations, testing, prescriptions, and referrals, specifically supporting people who are uninsured or unattached to a family provider and connecting them to ongoing services.
Solution: Community-run pop-up primary care clinics: Local nonprofits, faith groups, and volunteer clinicians organize regular pop-up clinics in community centres or schools to provide basic primary care, vaccinations, and referrals for residents who lack timely access to a family provider.

Description: The Stay Connected Mental Health Project partners with post-secondary campuses across Nova Scotia to train student leaders and peer ambassadors who normalize help-seeking and connect peers to supports. Through peer-led outreach, workshops, and campus support circles, the program reduces isolation and equips students with practical coping tools. Ambassadors actively signpost professional resources, streamline transitions to care, and coordinate with campus and provincial mental-health services.
Solution: Peer mental-health support networks: Trained peer volunteers from neighbourhoods, post-secondary institutions, and youth groups run in-person and online support circles that reduce isolation, provide coping strategies, and signpost professional resources.

Program: Borrow the Internet and Meeting Spaces
Description: Western Counties Regional Library lends mobile Wi‑Fi hotspots through its Borrow the Internet service and provides quiet rooms/meeting spaces in branches, enabling private and reliable connections for virtual health visits. Staff can help patrons get online and access video platforms, ensuring residents—especially in rural areas—can attend telemedicine or counselling appointments without connectivity or privacy obstacles.
Solution: Telehealth access hubs in libraries and community centres: Public spaces provide private booths, reliable internet, device loans, and staff assistance so people can attend virtual medical or counselling appointments without technology or privacy barriers.
Address: Isaiah W. Wilson Memorial Library (Yarmouth), 405 Main Street, Yarmouth, NS B5A 1G3

Program: Meeting Rooms, Wi‑Fi, and Tech Help
Description: South Shore Public Libraries offers free meeting rooms and quiet spaces with high‑speed Wi‑Fi, plus public computers and staff assistance, so community members can participate in virtual medical and mental health appointments. Select branches also lend devices (such as tablets or hotspots), reducing technology and privacy barriers for residents who need a secure place to meet with clinicians online.
Solution: Telehealth access hubs in libraries and community centres: Public spaces provide private booths, reliable internet, device loans, and staff assistance so people can attend virtual medical or counselling appointments without technology or privacy barriers.
Address: Margaret Hennigar Public Library, 135 North Park Street, Bridgewater, NS B4V 9B3

Description: Avalon Centre offers no-cost, trauma-informed counselling for survivors of sexualized violence, including youth and young adults. The program is underwritten by a donor-funded pool—corporate sponsors, service clubs, and individual donors alongside grants—so that short-term counselling is fully subsidized, reducing out-of-pocket costs and helping to alleviate long waitlists for mental health care.
Solution: Sliding-scale counselling fund supported by businesses and donors: A community-managed pool funded by local businesses, service clubs, and philanthropists subsidizes short-term counselling for students, young workers, and low-income residents to reduce waitlist pressure and out-of-pocket costs.
Address: 1526 Dresden Row, Suite 401, Halifax, NS B3J 3K3

Description: Second Story Women’s Centre provides free and sliding-scale counselling for women and gender-diverse people across Lunenburg County, including students and young workers. Backed by United Way support and a community-managed pool of donations from local businesses, service clubs, and individual philanthropists, the Centre subsidizes short-term counselling to minimize client fees and reduce strain on public mental health waitlists.
Solution: Sliding-scale counselling fund supported by businesses and donors: A community-managed pool funded by local businesses, service clubs, and philanthropists subsidizes short-term counselling for students, young workers, and low-income residents to reduce waitlist pressure and out-of-pocket costs.

Description: Farm Safety Nova Scotia delivers The Working Mind for Agriculture, an evidence-based mental health literacy and resilience program tailored to farmers, farm families, and agribusiness leaders. The program reduces stigma, teaches participants to spot early signs of distress, start supportive conversations, provide initial help, and refer to appropriate care and resources within rural communities.
Solution: Mental Health First Aid and resilience training: Widespread, volunteer-led training for teachers, employers, coaches, and community leaders builds local capacity to spot crises early, provide psychological first aid, and refer people to appropriate care.
Address: 60 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

Description: Construction Safety Nova Scotia convenes employers across the construction sector to improve psychological health and safety through training (e.g., mental health literacy and suicide prevention), policy guidance, and employer forums. The initiative promotes scheduling practices that reduce fatigue (e.g., staggered or compressed workweeks where feasible) and encourages supportive leave and return‑to‑work policies, helping member companies address burnout and retain younger workers.
Solution: Employer coalitions promoting flexible work and leave: Local businesses form coalitions to share best practices and jointly offer flexible schedules, compressed workweeks, and mental-health leave policies that reduce burnout and improve retention of young workers.
Address: 10 Ragged Lake Boulevard, Unit 12, Halifax, NS B3S 1R9

Program: Halifax North Memorial Community Wellness & Drop-In
Description: This branch functions as a community wellness hub, hosting free programs like meditation and yoga sessions, art and crafting circles, social and peer-support meetups with partner organizations, and health information workshops. The library provides open drop-in access, quiet and study rooms, and a community navigator to connect residents to mental-health and social supports.
Solution: Community wellness hubs and drop-in spaces: Neighbourhood centres provide low-cost activities—peer counselling, mindfulness, exercise classes, arts programs, and quiet rooms—so residents can access preventative mental-health supports close to home.

Description: Northwood offers pre-booked, door-to-door transportation that helps older adults and people with disabilities get to family doctors, specialists, counselling, and other health appointments. The service uses trained drivers and accessible vehicles to bridge transportation gaps, reducing missed visits and easing delays in care.
Solution: Volunteer transportation and ride-share for appointments: Volunteer driver programs and organized ride-share networks help people get to primary care and mental-health appointments, reducing missed visits and waitlist delays due to transportation barriers.

Description: Chebucto Family Centre offers parent-led playgroups and on-site child-minding/respite blocks so caregivers can attend appointments, rest, or participate in workshops without childcare barriers. By facilitating cooperative play sessions where families share setup and supervision and by providing low- or no-cost short-term care, the centre builds a neighbourhood support network that reduces caregiver burnout and helps young workers maintain stable schedules.
Solution: Community childcare co-ops to reduce caregiver burnout: Neighbourhood-run childcare co-ops and reciprocal care networks give parents and young workers reliable, affordable childcare so they can attend appointments, rest, or maintain stable work schedules.

Organization: Cole Harbour Rural Heritage Society (Cole Harbour Heritage Farm Museum)
Description: The Cole Harbour Heritage Farm Museum hosts community gardens, volunteer garden workdays, and hands-on horticulture workshops in a welcoming outdoor setting. These nature-based, social activities provide gentle physical activity and routine, reduce stress, and strengthen community ties—key protective factors that complement formal mental health and primary care.
Solution: Arts- and nature-based therapeutic programs: Local arts organizations and parks groups offer group music, art, and outdoor programs (guided hikes, gardening, forest bathing) that lower stress, build social connection, and complement clinical care.

Description: The Maritime Conservatory offers accessible group music-making for youth and adults—choirs, orchestras, bands, and community classes—that foster creativity and social connection. Regular rehearsals and performances provide structure, stress relief, and a sense of belonging, supporting mental wellbeing and complementing clinical care when needed.
Solution: Arts- and nature-based therapeutic programs: Local arts organizations and parks groups offer group music, art, and outdoor programs (guided hikes, gardening, forest bathing) that lower stress, build social connection, and complement clinical care.

Program: Nova Scotia Sexual Assault Provincial Helpline (Phone, Text & Chat)
Organization: 211 Nova Scotia (in partnership with the Government of Nova Scotia)
Description: A 24/7 confidential helpline that provides phone, text, and online chat support to anyone affected by sexual violence in Nova Scotia. Responders offer immediate emotional support, safety planning, and real-time referrals to local counselling, medical, legal, and community resources across the province. The always-on, multi-channel service ensures people can reach caring help after hours, easing pressure on emergency services and addressing acute loneliness and distress.
Solution: 24/7 volunteer helpline and text support: A locally staffed or partnered volunteer helpline and text/chat service provides immediate emotional support, crisis triage, and referrals outside normal office hours to reduce emergency burden and loneliness.
Address: 46 Portland Street, Suite 301, Dartmouth, NS B2Y 1H4

Description: Poparide is a Canada-wide ridesharing platform that actively serves Nova Scotia, matching drivers and passengers on common routes such as Halifax–Truro, Halifax–Sydney, and Halifax–Moncton. It implements the solution by providing verified profiles, ratings, in-app messaging, cost-splitting per seat, and route/time-based matching via web and mobile, enabling students, commuters, and event-goers to share rides and reduce travel costs. Employers and campus groups commonly promote consistent carp...
Solution: Community Ride-Sharing and Carpool Platform: Create a trusted, locally moderated ride-matching platform (web + SMS) for commuters, students, and event-goers that prioritizes safety, route-sharing, cost-splitting, and matches based on schedules and workplaces. Integrate with employers and campuses to promote consistent carpools.

Description: Kangaride is an intercity carpool platform operating across Canada, including Nova Scotia, that connects drivers and passengers for cost-shared trips based on route and schedule. It implements the solution by offering verified identities, phone confirmations, ratings, and transparent seat pricing, helping commuters, students, and event-goers safely coordinate shared rides via web and app. Organizations and campus communities use the platform to encourage recurring carpools by circulating grou...
Solution: Community Ride-Sharing and Carpool Platform: Create a trusted, locally moderated ride-matching platform (web + SMS) for commuters, students, and event-goers that prioritizes safety, route-sharing, cost-splitting, and matches based on schedules and workplaces. Integrate with employers and campuses to promote consistent carpools.
Address: 1650 Boulevard King Ouest, Suite 220, Sherbrooke, QC J1J 2C3

Organization: Cycling Nova Scotia (in partnership with Nova Scotia Department of Public Works and municipalities)
Description: Blue Route is a province-wide network of signed cycling corridors that connects communities across Nova Scotia through on-road bike routes and multi-use trails. Led by Cycling Nova Scotia with municipal and provincial partners, it maps priority inter-community corridors and delivers phased, low-cost upgrades like paved shoulders, wayfinding signage, and separated paths where needed, with municipalities establishing maintenance practices to support reliable year-round use on key segments.
Solution: Active Transport Networks and Bike Highways: Mobilize neighbourhood groups and municipal partners to map priority cycling and walking corridors between communities and key destinations, then deliver phased, low-cost infrastructure upgrades (painted lanes, signage, separated paths) and winter maintenance agreements to make active travel reliable year-round.
Address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

Organization: Town of Bridgewater – Engineering & Public Works
Description: The Town of Bridgewater’s Active Transportation Network identifies and phases priority walking and cycling corridors that connect residential areas with downtown, schools, and employment hubs. The town delivers low-cost infrastructure—painted bike lanes, multi-use paths, crossings, and wayfinding—and coordinates winter maintenance through Public Works so priority routes remain usable year-round.
Solution: Active Transport Networks and Bike Highways: Mobilize neighbourhood groups and municipal partners to map priority cycling and walking corridors between communities and key destinations, then deliver phased, low-cost infrastructure upgrades (painted lanes, signage, separated paths) and winter maintenance agreements to make active travel reliable year-round.

Description: The Cobequid Trail is a connected, multi-use active transportation corridor linking Bible Hill, Truro, and Salmon River with downtown and regional destinations. The Town of Truro and partners map and sign key segments, improve crossings and surfaces to support walking and cycling, and coordinate seasonal maintenance so sections remain accessible for reliable, year-round active travel.
Solution: Active Transport Networks and Bike Highways: Mobilize neighbourhood groups and municipal partners to map priority cycling and walking corridors between communities and key destinations, then deliver phased, low-cost infrastructure upgrades (painted lanes, signage, separated paths) and winter maintenance agreements to make active travel reliable year-round.

Program: Electrify Nova Scotia Rebate Program – E-bikes
Description: Administered by Clean Foundation (EV Assist) for the Province of Nova Scotia, this program offers rebates for eligible e-bikes, including cargo models, to reduce upfront purchase costs. By subsidizing e-bikes for residents across the province, it supports longer-distance commuting and everyday trips, complementing local lending libraries and repair co-ops to expand access to electric and active transportation.
Solution: Community Bike and E-Bike Libraries: Establish community-run bike/e-bike lending hubs and maintenance co-ops that provide affordable monthly rentals, repair training, and subsidized e-bikes for long-distance commuting, enabling more residents to use active and electric cargo bikes for daily trips.
Address: 126 Chain Lake Drive, Halifax, NS B3S 1A2

Description: Kings Point‑to‑Point Transit offers chartered and demand‑responsive group shuttles for local festivals, community events, and market days, and can schedule employer‑supported rides during seasonal employment peaks in the Annapolis Valley. By temporarily linking rural communities with venues and work sites, these services test new corridors, demonstrate latent demand, and help build the case for sustained, permanent routes.
Solution: Pop-up Event and Seasonal Shuttles: Organize temporary shuttles for festivals, market days, and seasonal employment peaks that connect isolated communities to cultural and job opportunities, demonstrating demand and building case studies for permanent services.
Address: 14 Crescent Drive, New Minas, NS B4N 3G7

Description: The Dal Bike Centre provides a do-it-yourself repair space, tool lending, refurbished parts, and regular maintenance workshops and tune‑up clinics that help campus and community cyclists keep their bikes in good condition. The Centre hires and trains student mechanics in paid roles to mentor peers and manage repair days—building practical skills and reducing operating costs while supporting everyday cycling as reliable transportation.
Solution: Community Transport Maintenance & Volunteer Repair Days: Organize regular volunteer maintenance days to keep community vehicles, bike lanes, and active transport facilities in good condition. Train local youth in vehicle and bike maintenance as paid apprenticeships that build skills and keep operating costs down.

Description: Saint Mary’s University’s Bike Room runs pop‑up repair days, fix‑it sessions, and hands‑on workshops that keep student and staff commuter bikes in safe working order. The space is staffed by trained student employees and volunteers who gain practical mechanic experience in paid on‑campus roles, strengthening a culture of active transportation while keeping maintenance affordable.
Solution: Community Transport Maintenance & Volunteer Repair Days: Organize regular volunteer maintenance days to keep community vehicles, bike lanes, and active transport facilities in good condition. Train local youth in vehicle and bike maintenance as paid apprenticeships that build skills and keep operating costs down.

Description: Maritime Bus operates a parcel express service that moves time-sensitive packages between communities across Nova Scotia and the Maritimes using space on scheduled passenger coaches. By consolidating small business shipments and parts for trades onto intercity bus routes (and connecting via regional ferries where applicable), it provides same-day/next-day ground delivery that reduces reliance on expensive air cargo for local commerce.
Solution: Local Freight and Courier Co-ops to Reduce Air Dependency: Form a regional courier or consolidated freight network for time-sensitive goods (parts for trades, small business shipments) that uses passenger shuttles, vans, and ferries to keep costs down and reduce dependence on expensive air cargo for local commerce.

Description: Chebucto Community Net is a volunteer-run community internet organization that provides low-cost access and hands-on help to residents and community groups in the Halifax area. Volunteers act as digital stewards by assisting users with configuring home routers, setting up secure Wi‑Fi networks, and troubleshooting connectivity; they have also supported community wireless hotspots through the Chebucto Wireless initiative. This neighbor-to-neighbor model lowers technical barriers for older adul...
Solution: Volunteer Digital Stewards and Installation Teams: Train local volunteers to help neighbours install routers, set up Wi‑Fi extenders, configure secure home networks and maintain local wireless hotspots. This lowers barriers for older residents and those with limited technical skills.
Address: Room 006, Chase Building, 6136 University Avenue, Halifax, NS B3H 4R2

Description: Bell Wholesale provides regulated access to Bell-owned poles, strand, and underground conduits throughout Nova Scotia under CRTC-approved support-structure tariffs. Carriers and ISPs can sign support-structure agreements to attach fiber/coax or place sub-ducts in existing conduit, coordinating with utilities and municipalities to share common routes. This shared infrastructure model reduces construction costs and enables multi‑provider builds into smaller and rural communities.
Solution: Shared Infrastructure Agreements (Poles, Conduits and Towers): Coordinate municipalities, utilities and landowners to enable shared access to poles, conduits and tower sites. Community groups can broker or manage agreements so multiple providers can cost-effectively extend service into rural areas.

Description: ROCK Networks (Nova Communications) designs and installs carrier-approved cellular signal boosters (e.g., Cel-Fi systems) and small-cell solutions in community halls, municipal buildings, health clinics, and other public facilities across Nova Scotia. They work with local stakeholders to survey sites, secure approvals, and deploy equipment, creating shared, community-sited improvements that extend reliable mobile coverage for residents, businesses, and emergency services.
Solution: Community Cell Boosters and Small‑Cell Deployments: Identify strategic community-owned locations (halls, water towers, municipal buildings) where small cellular nodes or signal boosters can be installed to improve mobile coverage. Organize permits, site stewardship and cost-sharing among users.

Description: Pictou-Antigonish Regional Library coordinates a bulk purchase of mobile Wi‑Fi hotspots (and complementary loaner devices) and distributes them through its branches for home use by residents. By aggregating demand and managing procurement centrally, the program lowers per-unit costs and accelerates adoption of home connectivity in rural communities across Pictou and Antigonish counties.
Solution: Bulk Purchasing Programs for Home Connectivity and Devices: Organize cooperative buying programs so households can purchase routers, extenders, antennas or low-cost ISP plans in bulk to lower per-unit costs and speed adoption. Local businesses or the municipality can coordinate procurement and distribution.
Address: 182 Dalhousie Street, New Glasgow, NS B2H 4M5

Organization: Municipality of the District of St. Mary’s
Description: The District of St. Mary’s convenes a citizen-and-municipal Connectivity Committee to gather local feedback, run connectivity surveys, and maintain an evidence-based inventory of underserved areas. This committee collaborates with ISPs and engages provincial and federal decision-makers to align funding applications and advocate for prioritized rural broadband and mobile projects across the municipality.
Solution: Advocacy and Coordinated Government Engagement: Form a citizen-led broadband advisory group to compile local evidence, prioritize projects, and engage municipal, provincial and federal decision-makers and funding streams with a unified voice and clear project proposals.

Program: Collaborative Procurement and Standing Offers (MASH Sector Access)
Organization: Province of Nova Scotia – Procurement (Service Nova Scotia and Internal Services)
Description: Nova Scotia’s Procurement division runs collaborative procurements and provincewide standing offers that can be used by provincial departments, Nova Scotia Health, IWK, regional centres for education, municipalities, and other MASH entities. By aggregating demand across these public buyers and awarding multi‑year, often regionalized contracts, the program creates predictable volumes that make it easier for small local suppliers to compete and win work through a single, streamlined agreement.
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Local Procurement Consortia: Form buyer consortia of schools, health centres and municipalities to aggregate demand and create predictable contracts that make it easier for small local suppliers to win work.

Program: Canadian Collaborative Procurement Initiative (CCPI) – Atlantic Region
Description: CCPI enables Nova Scotia’s municipalities, academic institutions, schools, and hospitals (MASH) to use federal standing offers and supply arrangements, pooling demand with other public buyers to secure stable pricing and service levels. This buyer consortium model reduces duplication of tenders and opens a clear pathway for qualified local small and medium suppliers to access predictable, consolidated contracts and receive call‑ups from multiple institutions.
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Local Procurement Consortia: Form buyer consortia of schools, health centres and municipalities to aggregate demand and create predictable contracts that make it easier for small local suppliers to win work.

Description: This voucher program gives small, non-dilutive grants (vouchers) to Nova Scotia SMEs to purchase R&D, prototyping, testing, and market-assessment services from local universities and colleges. It operates as a seed-stage catalyst by offsetting early validation and pilot costs, often leveraging company contributions and institutional resources—effectively matching public support with private effort to accelerate commercialization.
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Microgrant and Seed Match Programs: Community foundations, businesses and municipalities jointly fund small microgrants and match public seed funding for pre-revenue pilots, commercialization, and market validation.

Program: Credit Union Social Enterprise Loan Guarantee Program
Description: New Ross Credit Union participates in the Credit Union Social Enterprise Loan Guarantee Program, which pools a community-backed guarantee fund with provincial support to de-risk lending to early-stage and growing social enterprises. By using the guarantee to cover a significant portion of potential losses, the credit union can extend microloans and operating lines that enable impact-focused organizations to access affordable financing they wouldn’t secure from conventional lending alone.
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Community-backed Loan Guarantee Scheme: Pool a small guarantee fund through local stakeholders that reduces lender risk for microloans to early-stage businesses, unlocking credit from local credit unions and banks.

Program: Saint Mary’s University Entrepreneurship Centre – Coaching & Student Consulting
Organization: Saint Mary’s University Entrepreneurship Centre (SMUEC), Saint Mary’s University
Description: SMUEC offers training and advisory services that include crowdfunding education for startups and social enterprises, covering campaign planning, messaging, budgeting, and digital marketing tactics to activate local supporters. Through staff advisors and student consulting teams, founders receive practical help producing campaign assets (e.g., pitch pages and outreach plans) and can access in-kind promotion via SMUEC events and partner networks, strengthening both rewards- and equity-crowdfund...
Challenge: Barriers to Entrepreneurship and Access to Capital
Solution: Local Crowdfunding Campaign Support: Provide community workshops, coaching and in-kind marketing to help founders run successful rewards- or equity-crowdfunding campaigns that mobilize area supporters.

Program: Free Legal Clinic at the Halifax Law Courts
Organization: Nova Scotia Courts (in partnership with Pro Bono Nova Scotia)
Description: This clinic offers brief, pro bono legal advice from volunteer lawyers to self-represented people in civil and family matters, including administrative law issues. Lawyers help participants understand bylaws and regulations, prepare or review forms and affidavits, and discuss options to appeal or seek judicial review of government and municipal decisions. The service equips residents to navigate complex permitting or licensing processes and challenge adverse rulings.
Solution: Community Legal Clinic for Permits and Licensing: Create a pro‑bono clinic where volunteer planners and lawyers help residents appeal decisions, interpret bylaws, complete complex applications and navigate occupational licensing hurdles.
Address: 1815 Upper Water Street, Halifax, NS B3J 1S7

Program: Nova Scotia Works – Certification & Employment Supports
Organization: TEAM Work Cooperative and WorkBridge Association (Nova Scotia Works Centre)
Description: Nova Scotia Works centres can provide funding for short‑term training and required certifications, including exam and licensing fees needed to start work in trades and other regulated occupations for eligible low‑income jobseekers and youth. Through individualized employment plans and access to provincial Skills Development and related supports, clients receive bursary‑style assistance that removes cost barriers to meeting regulatory requirements.

Organization: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service (on behalf of the Affordable Energy Coalition)
Description: Dalhousie Legal Aid Service represents the Affordable Energy Coalition in Nova Scotia Utility and Review Board proceedings, coordinating community voices and evidence to improve electricity policy. Their interventions advocate for equitable, transparent fee design (including connection-related charges), consumer protections, and clearer, more predictable utility processes and timelines—supporting fair access to electrification and distributed renewables.
Challenge: Energy and Grid Constraints for Growth
Solution: Community Advocacy and Regional Coordination: Organize residents and businesses to advocate for prioritized intertie upgrades, fair interconnection fee structures and predictable timelines from provincial and utility authorities, leveraging consolidated local evidence and petitions.

Program: Town and County of Antigonish Joint Planning and Building Services
Organization: Town of Antigonish and Municipality of the County of Antigonish
Description: Through a shared-services agreement, the Town of Antigonish and the Municipality of the County of Antigonish operate a joint planning and building services team that harmonizes land-use policies, development review, and building inspection across urban and rural areas. The arrangement pools funding and professional capacity, coordinates growth management and active transportation planning, and creates a single interface for developers and residents, directly reducing governance silos.
Solution: Inter-Municipal Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs): Encourage neighbouring municipalities to sign simple MOUs to share services, coordinate land-use and transit planning, and pool funding for regional priorities, reducing policy fragmentation and improving efficiency for rural-urban linkages.
Address: 285 Beech Hill Road, Antigonish, NS B2G 0B4

Program: Kings Partnership Steering Committee (KPSC) / Kings 2050 Collaboration
Organization: Municipality of the County of Kings; Town of Berwick; Town of Kentville; Town of Wolfville
Description: KPSC is an inter-municipal forum established by agreement among the County of Kings and the Towns of Berwick, Kentville, and Wolfville to coordinate on shared services and regional planning. Through initiatives such as the Kings 2050 collaboration, partners align municipal planning strategies, coordinate regional transit and solid waste services, and pool resources for cross-boundary priorities, improving efficiency and reducing policy fragmentation across the Annapolis Valley’s rural and urb...
Solution: Inter-Municipal Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs): Encourage neighbouring municipalities to sign simple MOUs to share services, coordinate land-use and transit planning, and pool funding for regional priorities, reducing policy fragmentation and improving efficiency for rural-urban linkages.
Address: 181 Coldbrook Village Park Drive, Coldbrook, NS B4R 1B9

Organization: Town of Bridgewater (on behalf of municipal partners in Lunenburg County)
Description: TLC is a regional transit service delivered through an inter-municipal partnership that includes the Town of Bridgewater and neighboring municipal units, pooling municipal and provincial funding to run coordinated routes serving both urban and rural communities. The partnership aligns service design with land-use and economic nodes across municipal boundaries, creating a unified governance and planning table that reduces fragmentation in mobility planning and strengthens rural-urban connectiv...
Solution: Inter-Municipal Memoranda of Understanding (MOUs): Encourage neighbouring municipalities to sign simple MOUs to share services, coordinate land-use and transit planning, and pool funding for regional priorities, reducing policy fragmentation and improving efficiency for rural-urban linkages.

Organization: Clean Foundation (in partnership with the Province of Nova Scotia)
Description: Connect2 convenes municipalities, community groups, and the Province to plan and fund active transportation projects that link people to key destinations, often bridging rural communities with urban service centres. Acting as a facilitator and liaison, the program supports evidence-based project selection, provincial-municipal coordination, and integrated mobility planning—strengthening transit links and ensuring local priorities inform regional transportation strategies.
Solution: Rural-Urban Liaison Roles: Create volunteer or part-time liaison positions that connect rural communities with urban centres and provincial agencies to ensure priorities, transit links, and workforce pipelines are coordinated and that rural voices are reflected in regional planning.

Description: A volunteer‑driven, non‑profit food co‑operative that serves free/pay‑what‑you‑can plant‑based meals and hosts workshops and community events in the Dalhousie Student Union Building, creating an inclusive third‑place environment with seating and Wi‑Fi. Funds and donations are reinvested into programming, and the co‑op collaborates with campus and community groups to share space and resources at low or no cost.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Community-run café/co-op as a 'third place': Form a cooperative to open a volunteer-run café or social space offering affordable food, free wifi, meeting rooms, and cultural programming. Profits reinvested in programming and subsidized space rental for local groups.

Description: Held seasonally at the waterfront, the Creamery Square Night Market offers evening shopping with local producers, artisans, and food vendors alongside live entertainment. By programming markets after typical business hours and adding music and family-friendly activities, it provides a safe, social ‘night out’ that strengthens community life and supports small businesses.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Evening markets and extended-hours nights: Coordinate monthly evening markets, themed 'night out' events or late-shopping nights with local businesses, street performances, and family-friendly activities to create regular safe nightlife options.

Description: The Sport Fund offers seed microgrants to community sport organizations across Nova Scotia to start or expand low-cost sport and physical activity programs. Grants typically cover equipment, coaching training, and facility costs, which lowers financial barriers so local groups can deliver affordable leagues, try‑it sessions, and after‑school programs that engage children and youth in accessible recreation.
Challenge: Community Amenities and Vibrant Public Spaces
Solution: Affordable programming fund and microgrants: Establish a small community fund (crowdfunded + municipal match) to provide microgrants to grassroots organizers for festivals, sports leagues, youth nights, and other low-cost recreation initiatives.
Address: 5516 Spring Garden Road, 4th Floor, Halifax, NS B3J 1G6

Program: Nova Scotia Health – Summer Student Employment Program
Description: Nova Scotia Health hires high school and post-secondary students for paid summer roles in care and support settings (e.g., long-term care, nutrition & food services, environmental services, and clinical support). These placements provide practical experience, exposure to healthcare careers, and a pathway into further training and employment in the province’s care sector.
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: School-to-Work Pathways and Trade Camps: Partner with local schools to provide co-op placements, summer trade and care camps, and in-class modules so students get real work experience and clear pathways after graduation.

Description: Chebucto Family Centre offers free on-site childminding during workshops, programs, and support sessions so parents can attend training, appointments, and job-readiness activities. As a community-run hub, it coordinates childminding at varied times and connects families with local childcare options, easing access for those working or training in sectors with nonstandard schedules. This flexible, community-based model helps remove childcare barriers that can keep parents out of skilled trades ...
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: Community Childcare Co-operatives: Develop locally run, affordable childcare co-ops and flexible childminding networks so workers in care, construction, and trades can work nonstandard hours or attend training.

Organization: Nova Scotia College of Early Childhood Education
Description: NSCECE’s Mentor-Coach Program places highly experienced early childhood educators in part-time, on-site coaching roles to build the skills of newer staff and emerging leaders. These senior practitioners often use the program as a phased step toward retirement, maintaining reduced workloads while transferring institutional practices and quality standards. By stabilizing and upskilling childcare teams, the program helps expand capacity and retain local knowledge in the sector.
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: Phased Retirement and Knowledge-Transfer Program: Enable phased retirement arrangements where senior workers retain part-time mentoring roles while training successors, ensuring institutional knowledge stays local.

Description: Brilliant Labs delivers mobile and pop-up makerspaces across Nova Scotia, setting up temporary labs with 3D printers, electronics, sewing machines, and digital fabrication tools in rural schools and community centres. These sessions provide hands-on design, build, and repair experiences that cultivate practical skills relevant to skilled trades, technology, and creative industries.
Challenge: Workforce Shortages in Care, Construction, and Skilled Trades
Solution: Mobile Training Units and Pop-up Labs: Deploy mobile skill-training vans or pop-up maker spaces to reach rural and remote communities with hands-on trade and care training sessions.
Address: 5440 Spring Garden Road, Halifax, NS B3J 1E9

Organization: Dalhousie University Faculty of Computer Science (in partnership with the Province of Nova Scotia and community partners)
Description: Here We Code engages ambassadors — industry professionals, alumni, and returnees — to visit classrooms, appear on webinars, and participate in recruitment events showcasing technology education and careers in Nova Scotia. Ambassadors share authentic return-to-NS stories, pathways into tech, and work-life realities, directly addressing misconceptions about limited opportunity. By mentoring students and prospective returnees, they help channel talent back to Nova Scotia’s growing digital economy.
Solution: Returnee Ambassador Program: Recruit and train volunteers who previously left then returned to Nova Scotia to speak at schools, online panels and recruitment events; ambassadors offer realistic insights, mentor prospective returnees and counter negative narratives with firsthand accounts.

Program: Cape Breton Community Advisory Board on Homelessness (Reaching Home)
Description: Hosted by United Way Cape Breton, the CAB convenes residents, municipal staff, nonprofits, outreach teams, and property owners to coordinate rapid, practical housing solutions across the CBRM. It organizes information sessions and landlord-engagement initiatives, aligns funding toward quick-start affordable rentals and supportive options, and publicly shares progress—embodying a regional housing action coalition that builds confidence through visible, local solutions.
Solution: Housing Action Coalitions: Form neighborhood-level groups of residents, landlords, small developers and non-profits to identify quick wins on affordable rentals, co-op housing pilots and information sessions that demonstrate local commitment to realistic housing solutions.

Description: The Nova Scotia Co-operative Council supports communities to organize resident-led housing co-operatives by facilitating meetings with tenants, local nonprofits, municipal planners, and small developers. Through feasibility assessments, governance training, and public info sessions, the program helps launch co-op pilots and expand attainable rental options—directly implementing the solution’s coalition model for quick, realistic, community-backed housing wins.
Solution: Housing Action Coalitions: Form neighborhood-level groups of residents, landlords, small developers and non-profits to identify quick wins on affordable rentals, co-op housing pilots and information sessions that demonstrate local commitment to realistic housing solutions.
Address: 60 Research Drive, Bible Hill, NS B6L 2R2

Description: Atlantic Open Farm Day invites the public to visit participating Nova Scotia farms for guided tours, demonstrations, and conversations with producers. These behind-the-scenes workplace visits let residents and returnees experience rural livelihoods and agri-food innovation up close, dispelling myths about the sector and showcasing quality of life in farming communities across the province.
Solution: Neighbourhood Open Homes and Employer Tours: Host regular open-house events where residents tour workplaces, co-working spaces, maker spaces and sample neighborhoods to experience local workplaces and lifestyle firsthand, dismantling misconceptions through direct exposure.
Address: 7 Atlantic Central Drive, East Mountain, NS B6L 2Z2

Program: Lunenburg Region Partners for Economic Prosperity (LRPEP)
Organization: Lunenburg Region Partners for Economic Prosperity
Description: LRPEP is a multi-municipal partnership (Municipality of the District of Lunenburg, Towns of Bridgewater, Lunenburg, and Mahone Bay) working with businesses and non-profits to build and manage the unified Lunenburg Region brand. By pooling municipal and private-sector resources, LRPEP delivers consistent regional messaging, brand assets, and campaigns that highlight local strengths—entrepreneurship, trades, ocean tech, and arts—and uses data-informed stories to counter misconceptions about opp...
Solution: Regional Brand Cooperative: Create a community-led cooperative of municipalities, businesses, non-profits and cultural groups to pool modest funds and coordinate consistent messaging, visuals and campaigns that celebrate local strengths and correct misinformation.

Description: The Hants County Exhibition is a multi-day agricultural fair that features 4-H youth competitions, local food vendors, artisans, and machinery/trades demonstrations. It brings together young people, entrepreneurs, and employers in agriculture and related trades to exhibit projects, sell products, and recruit, celebrating rural innovation and opportunity in Nova Scotia.
Solution: Community Festivals that Showcase Opportunity: Build festivals or pop-up markets focused on local innovation, trades, arts and food where young people can exhibit projects, entrepreneurs can pitch ideas and employers can recruit, making opportunity visible and celebratory.

Organization: Construction Association of Nova Scotia (in partnership with Nova Scotia Apprenticeship Agency and the Nova Scotia Department of Education and Early Childhood Development)
Description: BFY enlists construction-sector employers to host paid, mentored summer placements for Grade 11 students, with employers committing to safe worksites, skill development, and pathways into registered apprenticeship. Participating companies are publicly recognized by the program and industry partners, signaling a youth-friendly workplace and helping them attract emerging talent while enhancing the region’s reputation for career-ready opportunities.
Solution: Community Employer Pledge and Recognition: Invite local businesses to sign a public pledge on hiring youth, offering clear career pathways and supporting flexible arrangements; recognize participants with a community-backed seal to build trust and attract talent.
Address: 260 Brownlow Avenue, Unit 3, Dartmouth, NS B3B 1V9

Organization: Ecology Action Centre (in partnership with Halifax Regional Municipality)
Description: The Mobile Food Market partners with local growers and wholesalers to bulk-purchase produce and sell it at pop-up markets in communities across Halifax at reduced prices. By aggregating supply and operating weekly or biweekly markets, it offers affordable produce packs and staples, increasing access to healthy food for youth, seniors, and families facing high grocery costs. The initiative functions like a community buying club on wheels, bringing low-cost essentials directly to neighborhoods.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Food Co-op and Bulk-Buy Program: A member-run grocery co-op that aggregates bulk purchases from regional suppliers (including Maritime producers) to lower grocery costs, offers sliding-scale memberships for youth, and hosts weekly low-cost pantry staples distribution.

Description: Noggins Corner Farm organizes charity harvest and gleaning days where volunteers help collect surplus produce from their fields for donation to local food programs and food banks. By channeling post-harvest excess to community hubs like Feed Nova Scotia and neighborhood agencies, the farm reduces food waste and expands access to fresh fruits and vegetables for families facing high grocery costs.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Gardens, Gleaning Networks and Farm Partnerships: Neighbourhood gardens on municipal or church land, paired with gleaning programs that collect surplus from local farms and distribute it through community hubs, increasing access to fresh produce and reducing grocery bills.

Description: Loaves and Fishes operates a community kitchen and dining room that serves daily free or very low-cost hot meals in downtown Sydney. Using donated and surplus food and volunteer prep in a commercial kitchen, the program reduces waste, provides shared meals, and offers opportunities to build practical kitchen skills.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Community Kitchens and Shared Meal Programs: Shared commercial kitchen hours, meal prep co-ops, and pay-what-you-can community dinners run by local organizations to lower meal costs, build skills, and reduce food waste.

Program: Child Safety Link Helmet Bulk Purchase Program
Organization: IWK Health Centre – Child Safety Link
Description: Child Safety Link coordinates a bulk‑purchasing program that enables schools, youth groups, and community agencies to order CSA‑approved bicycle helmets at discounted prices. It also provides fit clinics and safety resources that complement community cycling initiatives and bike libraries, lowering the cost of essential protective gear for riders. This addresses the group‑purchasing component of the solution, making safe, everyday cycling more affordable.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Bike Libraries and Active-Transportation Hubs: Loaner bike programs, community bike repair cafés, and mapped safe routes to encourage cycling as an affordable commute option, paired with group purchasing of helmets and lights.

Program: NSGEU Group Home, Auto & Tenant Insurance Program
Organization: Nova Scotia Government & General Employees Union (NSGEU)
Description: NSGEU negotiates preferred group rates on home, auto, and tenant insurance for members through a national insurer partner and local brokers, lowering everyday insurance costs. The union regularly hosts on-site and virtual clinics with insurance representatives to help members compare coverage, access discounts, and receive practical claims advice.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Group Insurance Pools and Broker Clinics: Local associations (youth chambers, co-ops, freelancer networks) negotiate group rates for auto, renter's and small-business insurance; host clinics with brokers to compare low-cost coverage and claims advice.
Address: 255 John Savage Avenue, Dartmouth, NS B3B 0J3

Program: NSNU Member Home & Auto Group Insurance
Description: The Nova Scotia Nurses’ Union offers members group-rated home, auto, and tenant insurance through an affinity partnership, using pooled purchasing power to reduce premiums. NSNU complements the discount program with broker/advisor-led information sessions and webinars that walk members through coverage comparisons, savings options, and claims support.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Group Insurance Pools and Broker Clinics: Local associations (youth chambers, co-ops, freelancer networks) negotiate group rates for auto, renter's and small-business insurance; host clinics with brokers to compare low-cost coverage and claims advice.

Program: SMU Alumni Insurance Program (Home, Auto & Tenant)
Description: Saint Mary’s University Alumni Association partners with a national insurer to provide alumni in Nova Scotia with affinity group rates on home, tenant, and auto insurance, helping graduates manage cost-of-living pressures. The alumni office periodically coordinates broker/advisor info sessions and webinars so members can compare policies, understand coverage trade-offs, and get claims guidance.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Group Insurance Pools and Broker Clinics: Local associations (youth chambers, co-ops, freelancer networks) negotiate group rates for auto, renter's and small-business insurance; host clinics with brokers to compare low-cost coverage and claims advice.

Description: The YMCA’s licensed Family Home Child Care program recruits, trains, and supports approved home child care providers and matches them with families seeking small-group care. By enabling multiple families to share a single caregiver in a home setting and to arrange part‑time or non‑standard hours, the network lowers per‑family costs and offers flexible, community‑based options that align with cooperative and shared childminding models for working parents.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Cooperative Childcare and Shared Nanny Networks: Parent-run childcare co-ops, shared nanny/childminding networks and time-share childcare arrangements that lower childcare costs and increase flexible, community-based options for working young parents.

Organization: Saint Mary’s University – The Spark Zone Sandbox
Description: The Spark Zone is a university-led incubator that provides free co-working space, mentorship, workshops, and small seed funding to help students and recent graduates validate ideas and build early-stage ventures. By covering essentials like workspace, coaching, and prototype micro-grants, it reduces startup costs and risk for emerging entrepreneurs.
Challenge: Cost of Living Pressures Beyond Housing
Solution: Micro-Grants, Incubators and Co‑Working for Young Entrepreneurs: Community-managed micro-grants, low-cost co-working spaces, equipment libraries and mentorship programs that reduce startup costs for small businesses and side hustles.
